questions.scenario: Priya, an operations coordinator at Acme Logistics, types "Write something about the new warehouse shift rota" into Claude. The draft is generic, too long and aimed at no one in particular. She needs a 150-word notice for forklift drivers explaining that night shifts move from 22:00 to 21:00 starting 3 March.
questions.question: Which revised prompt is most likely to produce a usable notice on the first attempt?

options.A: "Write a polished, professional notice about the changes to the warehouse shift rota. Make it excellent, engaging and clear so that everybody understands it."
options.B: "Write about the rota. If it is wrong I will ask again."
options.C: "Write a 150-word notice for forklift drivers: night shift starts 21:00 instead of 22:00 from 3 March. Friendly, direct tone; end with the shift supervisor as the contact."
options.D: "You are the world's best internal communications expert with 20 years of logistics experience. Write about the new shift rota."

questions.explanation: Effective prompts state the audience, the purpose, the key facts, the length and the tone. Treat Claude like a capable new colleague who has no background: everything it needs to get the task right should be in the request. Adjectives such as "excellent" or an inflated role do not substitute for concrete requirements.

why_incorrect.A: Adding praise words does not supply the missing facts, audience, length or tone, so Claude still has to guess.
why_incorrect.B: Planning to retry instead of stating requirements wastes turns; the gaps are predictable and can be closed up front.
why_incorrect.D: A grand role without the actual details (who, what changed, when, how long) leaves the same gaps as the original prompt.

questions.scenario: A marketing lead at Fabrikam Retail pastes a 12-page brand guideline and a product brief into one message, followed by "Use the guideline to write three taglines for the brief." Claude sometimes confuses which text is the guideline and which is the brief.
questions.question: What is the simplest change that helps Claude keep the two documents apart?

options.A: Wrap each document in labelled tags such as <brand_guideline> and <product_brief>, and refer to those labels in the instruction.
options.B: Put the instruction in capital letters at the very top and repeat it at the bottom, so that it stands out clearly from both documents.
options.C: Paste the two documents in two separate chats and ask Claude to combine them later.
options.D: Remove the long brand guideline and rely on Claude's general knowledge of Fabrikam's tone, which keeps the prompt short and focused.

questions.explanation: When a prompt mixes instructions with several pieces of reference material, labelled delimiters such as XML-style tags make the structure explicit. Claude can then follow instructions like "apply the tone rules in <brand_guideline> to <product_brief>" without mixing the sources up.

why_incorrect.B: Emphasis does not tell Claude where one document ends and the other begins; clear delimiters do.
why_incorrect.C: Claude cannot see a different chat's content unless it is brought into the conversation, so this breaks the task rather than clarifying it.
why_incorrect.D: Claude has no reliable knowledge of a fictional company's internal brand rules; removing the source lowers accuracy.

questions.scenario: Daniel, an HR business partner at Northwind Lending, wants Claude to draft interview questions for a junior data analyst role. His first prompt, "Give me interview questions for an analyst", returned 30 generic questions covering roles he does not hire for.
questions.question: Which TWO additions to his prompt would most improve the relevance of the output?

options.A: A note that the hiring manager will review the output, so that Claude raises its standard and filters out generic questions.
options.B: A request that Claude "think harder than usual" and take extra care, so that it reasons more deeply about which questions fit the role.
options.C: The names and CVs of the candidates who have applied so far.
options.D: The format he needs, such as eight behavioural questions with a short note on what a strong answer shows.
options.E: The job description's key responsibilities and the three competencies the panel must assess.

questions.explanation: Relevance comes from context (what the role actually involves and what must be assessed) and from a defined output format (how many questions, what type, what supporting notes). Both remove guesswork. Extra effort requests and reviewer notes do not supply the missing information, and candidate CVs introduce personal data without improving the questions.

why_incorrect.A: Knowing there will be a reviewer does not give Claude the role context or format that drive relevance.
why_incorrect.B: Asking for more effort does not tell Claude which role, level or competencies matter, which is the actual gap.
why_incorrect.C: Candidate personal data is not needed to write role-based questions and adds unnecessary privacy risk.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health's patient-experience team wants Claude to rewrite appointment reminders in a warm but concise style. They have written a long description of the style, but Claude's rewrites still feel stiff.
questions.question: What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Add two or three short before-and-after examples of reminders rewritten in the desired style, labelled as examples.
options.B: Remove the style description and simply ask Claude to make the reminders sound friendlier.
options.C: Tell Claude to imitate the voice of a well-known author famous for warmth, so it has a recognisable style to follow.
options.D: Expand the style description to twice its length with more adjectives, so that every nuance of "warm but concise" is spelled out.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples are one of the most reliable ways to communicate tone and format. A small set of varied, clearly labelled examples shows Claude what "warm but concise" means for this team, which descriptive adjectives struggle to do.

why_incorrect.B: A vaguer request moves further from the specific target; Claude has even less to go on than before.
why_incorrect.C: An unrelated literary voice is unlikely to match a concise healthcare reminder and adds a new source of variation.
why_incorrect.D: More adjectives tend to stay abstract; concrete examples show the target style far more precisely.

questions.scenario: A project manager at Tailspin Travel gives Claude one example status update and asks for weekly updates for six different projects. Every update Claude writes copies the example's three-bullet structure and even reuses its phrase "slight slippage on vendor sign-off", including for projects that have no vendor.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause, and the best fix?

options.A: The model is too small to generalise from an example; switch to the largest available model and keep the same single example.
options.B: Remove the example and describe the format in words instead, since examples tend to be copied too literally.
options.C: One example is being over-imitated; give several varied examples and say they show format, not content to reuse.
options.D: Claude has run out of context after the first update; start a new chat for each project so each one has full room.

questions.explanation: Claude pays close attention to examples. With only one, it may treat incidental details as requirements. Using several diverse examples and saying what they are meant to demonstrate lets Claude generalise the pattern without copying specific wording.

why_incorrect.A: Larger models can also mirror a lone example closely; the cause is the narrow example set, not model size.
why_incorrect.B: Examples are very effective for format; the problem is having just one, and dropping examples loses their benefit.
why_incorrect.D: Six short updates are nowhere near a context limit, and the copying happens from the first update onwards.

questions.scenario: Mei, a programme manager at Proseware Education, asks Claude in one message to analyse 40 pages of course feedback, identify the top themes, propose fixes, draft an email to faculty and build a slide outline. The result is shallow in every part.
questions.question: What approach is most likely to improve quality?

options.A: Ask Claude to keep every part shorter and more concise, so it has room to cover all five deliverables in one response.
options.B: Send the same all-in-one prompt again, since outputs vary between attempts and a second run is likely to go deeper.
options.C: Split the work into sequential steps (themes, then fixes, then email and outline), checking each output before the next.
options.D: Remove the feedback document and describe the themes from memory instead.

questions.explanation: Complex, multi-stage requests usually work better as a chain of focused sub-tasks. Each step gets Claude's full attention, you can check intermediate results (for example the theme list) before building on them, and errors are caught early instead of spreading.

why_incorrect.A: Shorter output makes each part even shallower; the problem is depth, not length.
why_incorrect.B: Rerunning an overloaded prompt does not address the cause, which is too many distinct tasks competing in one response.
why_incorrect.D: Discarding the source data removes the evidence the analysis depends on.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's internal communications team is planning a quarterly town-hall pack with Claude: a summary of employee survey results, a Q&A list, and a speaker script that must reflect both.
questions.question: Which TWO decomposition decisions are sound?

options.A: Do the three in one prompt so they share the same context and stay consistent with each other.
options.B: Draft the Q&A list and the script as separate steps that each receive the approved summary as input.
options.C: Produce and validate the survey summary first, because the Q&A list and script both depend on it.
options.D: Write the speaker script first, because it sets the narrative, then derive the survey summary and Q&A list from what the script says.
options.E: Split the survey file into random chunks and ask a different chat to summarise each without combining them.

questions.explanation: Good decomposition follows the dependencies in the work. Upstream outputs that others rely on (the survey summary) come first and are checked, then downstream tasks each receive that verified input. This keeps the pack consistent and makes it easy to rework one piece without redoing everything.

why_incorrect.A: A single prompt does not make the outputs consistent or checkable; an approved shared summary is what keeps later outputs aligned.
why_incorrect.D: This reverses the dependency: the script should be grounded in the survey data, not the other way round.
why_incorrect.E: Uncombined fragments cannot produce one coherent summary for later steps to rely on.

questions.scenario: An events manager at Wingtip Events wants Claude's help choosing a venue for a 300-person conference. She has a shortlist of five venues, a budget and accessibility requirements.
questions.question: Which sequence of sub-tasks is the most sensible way to structure the work with Claude?

options.A: Ask Claude for a recommendation email first, and compile the comparison only if someone questions it.
options.B: Ask Claude to pick the best venue immediately, then ask it to explain the criteria afterwards.
options.C: Agree criteria and weights, compare each venue against them in a table, then draft a recommendation with trade-offs.
options.D: Ask for five separate, detailed venue descriptions so she can read them all and form her own overall view of which feels right.

questions.explanation: For decision tasks, decompose into: define criteria, evaluate options against them, then recommend. The structure makes the reasoning visible, lets the manager adjust weights, and produces a recommendation that stakeholders can check.

why_incorrect.A: Producing the conclusion before the analysis skips the step that makes the recommendation defensible.
why_incorrect.B: Deciding before defining criteria invites a post-hoc justification rather than a fair comparison.
why_incorrect.D: Without common criteria, the descriptions cannot be compared on a like-for-like basis.

questions.scenario: Rahul at Adatum Insurance chained three steps with Claude: extract key clauses from a supplier contract, flag unusual terms, then draft a summary for procurement. The final summary misses an auto-renewal clause, even though the flagging step looked reasonable.
questions.question: Where should Rahul look first?

options.A: The model used for the summary step, since a lighter model may have dropped less prominent clauses.
options.B: Chained prompts tend to lose information at hand-offs, so he should merge the three steps into one prompt and re-run it.
options.C: The output of the first extraction step, because a clause omitted there could never reach the later steps.
options.D: The summary step's tone and length instructions, because a strict word limit there could have squeezed the clause out of the final text.

questions.explanation: In a chain, each step only sees what earlier steps passed on. When something is missing at the end, trace backwards and check the earliest step that should have captured it. Inspecting intermediate outputs is a key benefit of decomposition.

why_incorrect.A: Changing the last step cannot recover information that was dropped earlier in the chain; the earliest step must be checked first.
why_incorrect.B: Chaining is useful precisely because each stage can be inspected; merging the steps removes that advantage without finding the cause.
why_incorrect.D: Tone and length settings in the last step cannot explain why the clause is missing from every step after extraction.

questions.scenario: A team lead at Litware Publishing is learning to use Claude for larger assignments and asks why colleagues recommend splitting big tasks into smaller prompts.
questions.question: Which statement best describes the main benefit?

options.A: Splitting tasks means each part is simple enough that the combined result no longer needs any human review.
options.B: Smaller prompts are needed because any prompt over a page long will exceed the context window and be cut off.
options.C: Claude tends to follow just the first instruction in a long prompt, so later requests in the same message are often ignored.
options.D: Each focused step is easier for Claude to do well and easier for a person to check before the next one builds on it.

questions.explanation: Decomposition improves quality by giving each sub-task full attention and makes errors visible at intermediate checkpoints. It is a quality and control technique, not a workaround for a hard rule about single instructions.

why_incorrect.A: Decomposition creates natural review points; it does not remove the need for human judgement.
why_incorrect.B: A one-page prompt is far below current context windows; quality and checkability, not hard limits, are the usual reasons to decompose.
why_incorrect.C: Claude can follow several instructions in one prompt; decomposition helps when sub-tasks are distinct and depend on each other.

questions.scenario: Sofia at Fourth Coffee asked Claude for a store-opening press release. The draft is good but uses US spelling and is 600 words; she needs British spelling and 300 words.
questions.question: What is the most efficient next message?

options.A: Start a new chat and paste the original prompt again unchanged, so Claude produces a fresh draft without the earlier context.
options.B: Edit the draft manually herself and not mention the spelling or length preferences, since Claude would likely repeat the mistake.
options.C: "Good structure. Please switch to British spelling and cut to about 300 words, keeping the opening quote and address paragraph."
options.D: "This isn't what I wanted, please try again and make it better."

questions.explanation: Iteration works best when feedback is specific: say what to keep, what to change and the target (spelling convention, length). Claude can then make a focused revision instead of starting over.

why_incorrect.A: The same prompt will likely produce the same issues because the missing requirements were never stated.
why_incorrect.B: Manual editing works once, but the preferences are lost for the rest of the conversation and future drafts.
why_incorrect.D: Vague negative feedback does not say what to change, so the next draft may lose what was already good.

questions.scenario: Over a week, Kenji at Relecloud has refined a prompt that turns meeting notes into action-item lists. Some revisions improved results and others made them worse, and he can no longer tell which change did what.
questions.question: Which TWO practices would make his iteration more reliable?

options.A: Test each new version on a different, freshly chosen set of notes, so that every version is judged against a wide variety of real meetings.
options.B: Judge each version on a single run and keep whichever reads best at a glance.
options.C: Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch every time a result disappoints.
options.D: Keep a simple log of each prompt version and what improved or got worse.
options.E: Change one element of the prompt at a time and compare outputs on the same set of sample notes.

questions.explanation: Treat prompt iteration like a small experiment: hold the test inputs constant, vary one thing, and record the outcome. This turns trial and error into evidence about which instructions actually help.

why_incorrect.A: Changing the inputs and the prompt together makes it impossible to tell which caused a difference.
why_incorrect.B: One impression is noisy; outputs vary, so comparisons need a few consistent test cases.
why_incorrect.C: Full rewrites change many variables at once and discard improvements that were working.

questions.scenario: A sales operations analyst at VanArsdel Foods asks Claude to summarise win/loss interview notes. The summaries are accurate but mostly restate what each customer said rather than drawing out patterns.
questions.question: Which refinement best targets the gap?

options.A: Add the instruction "be insightful" at the end of the prompt.
options.B: Ask Claude to make each individual interview summary shorter and tighter, so that the key point of each one stands out more clearly.
options.C: Ask explicitly for cross-interview patterns: recurring win and loss reasons, how often each appears, and a quote for each.
options.D: Ask Claude to rewrite the summaries in more formal, executive-ready language suitable for the sales leadership team.

questions.explanation: When output is correct but not useful, the prompt usually asked for the wrong task. Refine by naming the analysis you want (patterns, frequency, evidence) so Claude knows to synthesise across sources rather than summarise each one.

why_incorrect.A: A vague quality word does not specify what kind of synthesis is wanted.
why_incorrect.B: Shorter per-interview summaries are still per-interview; they do not create cross-interview analysis.
why_incorrect.D: Register has nothing to do with whether patterns are identified.

questions.scenario: After ten rounds of feedback in one long chat, a policy writer at Humongous Insurance notices Claude's drafts now mix instructions from early turns that she later reversed, such as an abandoned bullet-point format.
questions.question: What is the best way to continue iterating?

options.A: Keep going in the same chat and add a clear message listing which earlier instructions Claude should now ignore.
options.B: Delete the draft and write it manually because Claude cannot handle revisions.
options.C: Switch to a faster model for the remaining rounds, since a quicker model responds more directly to each new piece of feedback.
options.D: Ask Claude to summarise the agreed requirements, correct that summary, and continue in a fresh chat with it and the latest draft.

questions.explanation: Long iterative threads can accumulate superseded instructions. Consolidating the agreed requirements into a single, corrected brief and continuing in a fresh conversation gives Claude one clear source of truth.

why_incorrect.A: Piling up contradictory turns makes the conversation harder to follow, which is the source of the problem.
why_incorrect.B: Claude handles revisions well when the requirements are clear; the issue is accumulated, contradictory history.
why_incorrect.C: Speed does not resolve conflicting instructions accumulated in the conversation history.

questions.scenario: The innovation team at Coho Winery wants Claude's help naming a new low-alcohol sparkling wine. In a first session they asked for "the best name" and got one safe option.
questions.question: How should they adapt the prompt for a brainstorming task?

options.A: Give Claude a strict naming template (two syllables, starting with "C") that every suggestion must match exactly.
options.B: Ask for many varied options in different styles (playful, heritage, botanical), then shortlist and refine the best.
options.C: Ask again for one name, but specify the brand values and stress that it must be the single strongest possible choice.
options.D: Ask Claude to cite sources proving each name will sell well.

questions.explanation: Different task types need different prompts. Brainstorming rewards volume and diversity first, then convergence in a later step. Analysis and factual tasks, by contrast, reward precision, constraints and evidence.

why_incorrect.A: A rigid template suppresses the variety that makes brainstorming useful.
why_incorrect.C: Brainstorming benefits from breadth; asking for one "best" answer narrows the space too early.
why_incorrect.D: Sales evidence for new invented names does not exist, so this invites fabricated support.

questions.scenario: Leila, a policy analyst at Bellows College, needs a briefing on how three peer institutions handle remote-work policies for staff. The information is spread across several public web pages that change over time.
questions.question: Which approach best fits this research task?

options.A: Use research or web search, ask for a source for each claim, then check the key sources herself.
options.B: Ask Claude to write the briefing in the style of a news article without sources.
options.C: Ask Claude to brainstorm what the three policies probably say, then circulate the result for colleagues to correct.
options.D: Ask Claude in a plain chat to describe each peer's current policy in detail, since it has read a great deal about universities.

questions.explanation: Research tasks about current, external facts call for tools that retrieve live sources, an explicit request for citations, and a verification step. Plain chat relies on training data, which can be out of date for specific organisations.

why_incorrect.B: Dropping sources makes it impossible to verify claims in a research task.
why_incorrect.C: Brainstorming generates possibilities, not verified facts about what institutions actually do.
why_incorrect.D: Training data has a cutoff and may be incomplete or outdated for specific institutional policies.

questions.scenario: A strategy manager at Trey Research uses Claude for four kinds of work: analysing a dataset of churn reasons, researching competitor pricing, drafting a board letter, and generating campaign ideas.
questions.question: Which THREE pairings of task type and prompting emphasis are appropriate?

options.A: Drafting: ask for as many alternative versions of the board letter as possible, without stating the audience, so that Claude explores widely.
options.B: Research: ask Claude to drop source links and citations so the summary reads smoothly and can be pasted straight into a report.
options.C: Brainstorming: request many diverse options before narrowing down.
options.D: Analysis: give the data, define the question, and ask Claude to show its reasoning and state uncertainties.
options.E: Drafting: specify audience, purpose, tone, length and any must-include points.

questions.explanation: Matching prompting style to task type is a core skill. Analysis benefits from clear questions and visible reasoning; drafting from audience and constraints; brainstorming from breadth; and research from sources and verification.

why_incorrect.A: Without an audience and purpose, the drafts cannot be judged against a goal; volume alone does not help a board letter.
why_incorrect.B: Research needs sources so claims can be checked; removing them undermines the task's purpose.

questions.scenario: An operations analyst at Alpine Ski House asks Claude why lift-ticket revenue dropped 12% in February, attaching daily sales and weather data. Claude's first answer confidently blames one factor.
questions.question: Which follow-up prompt better suits an analysis task?

options.A: Ask Claude to answer in one sentence to avoid overthinking.
options.B: Ask for ten creative marketing ideas to recover February's lost revenue, since the cause has already been identified.
options.C: Ask Claude to weigh several possible explanations against the data and rate how strongly the evidence supports each.
options.D: Ask Claude to rewrite its answer in a more persuasive, confident tone so it is ready to present to the leadership team.

questions.explanation: For analysis, ask Claude to weigh competing hypotheses against the evidence and to be explicit about confidence. This reduces premature conclusions and gives the analyst something they can verify.

why_incorrect.A: Constraining the answer to one sentence discourages the reasoning that analysis needs.
why_incorrect.B: This jumps to brainstorming solutions before the cause has been analysed.
why_incorrect.D: Persuasion polishes the conclusion but does nothing to check whether it is right.

questions.scenario: Claude summarised a 20-page vendor proposal for Ana, a procurement officer at Fabrikam Retail. The summary reads well, but she must send it to the approval committee today.
questions.question: What is the most effective way for Ana to evaluate the summary's completeness?

options.A: Check that the summary is grammatically correct and well formatted.
options.B: Ask Claude in the same chat whether the summary is complete and accurate, and send it once Claude confirms that it is.
options.C: Check that the summary is roughly one page, since a one-page summary of a 20-page proposal is the usual completeness benchmark.
options.D: Check the summary against a list of what the committee needs (price, term, service levels, exit terms), confirming each in the proposal.

questions.explanation: Completeness is judged against the reader's needs. A short checklist of required elements, each confirmed in the source document, is a fast, repeatable way to catch omissions before a decision is made on the summary.

why_incorrect.A: Polish says nothing about whether important content was left out.
why_incorrect.B: Self-assessment can help but is not independent; Claude may confidently confirm an incomplete summary.
why_incorrect.C: Every summary is shorter; length is not a measure of completeness.

questions.scenario: Claude produced a competitor feature comparison table for Southridge Video's product team, using public web pages gathered with web search.
questions.question: Which TWO checks most directly test the table's accuracy?

options.A: Check that every row and column is filled in, since an empty or inconsistent cell is the usual sign that a source was misread.
options.B: Confirm the table uses the company's brand colours.
options.C: Open the cited sources for a sample of cells, especially surprising ones, and confirm they say what the table claims.
options.D: Ask Claude to regenerate the table in a new chat and compare it with the first; cells that match in both versions can be treated as verified.
options.E: Check source dates, because competitor features and prices change and older pages may be out of date.

questions.explanation: Accuracy checks go back to evidence: verify claims against the cited sources, prioritising surprising or high-impact cells, and confirm the sources are current. Formatting and regeneration do not test truth.

why_incorrect.A: Consistent structure is about formatting, not whether the facts in the cells are true.
why_incorrect.B: Visual styling has no bearing on accuracy.
why_incorrect.D: Two similar outputs can both be wrong; consistency is not the same as accuracy.

questions.scenario: Claude extracted action items from a two-hour project meeting transcript for Contoso Health. A team member points out that two commitments made near the end of the meeting are missing.
questions.question: What is the most useful next step?

options.A: Ask Claude to work through the transcript section by section, quoting the line behind each action item, re-checking the end.
options.B: Ask Claude to add two further plausible action items to the list, based on the overall themes of the meeting.
options.C: Accept the list as it stands, since Claude rarely misses items and the two missing commitments may have been informal remarks.
options.D: Reduce the transcript to the first hour to make it easier.

questions.explanation: When output may be incomplete, ask Claude to ground each item in a quoted passage and to work systematically through the source. Quotes make each item verifiable and a section-by-section pass reduces skipped content in long inputs.

why_incorrect.B: Inventing items to fill a gap creates fabricated commitments instead of finding the real ones.
why_incorrect.C: A known gap has already been reported; it should be fixed rather than dismissed.
why_incorrect.D: The missing items are near the end; cutting the transcript would remove them entirely.

questions.scenario: A finance analyst at Northwind Lending asks Claude to total quarterly travel expenses from an uploaded CSV and explain the trend. The narrative is convincing, but she needs the numbers to be exact.
questions.question: What is the most reliable way to validate the figures?

options.A: Ask Claude to recheck its totals in the same chat, and accept them if it reports the same figures a second time.
options.B: Ask Claude to restate the totals with more decimal places.
options.C: Trust the figures because the narrative is internally consistent, and a consistent explanation of the trend is good evidence the totals are right.
options.D: Recompute the totals independently (a spreadsheet formula or Claude's analysis tool) and reconcile any differences.

questions.explanation: Numbers that will be reported should be checked by an independent calculation. Computed results (from a spreadsheet or code execution) are more dependable than figures produced in prose, and reconciling the two catches mistakes.

why_incorrect.A: Asking the same chat to recheck is not independent; a repeated figure can repeat the same mistake.
why_incorrect.B: More precision in the display does not make an incorrect sum correct.
why_incorrect.C: A coherent story can sit on top of an arithmetic mistake; consistency of narrative does not prove the numbers.

questions.scenario: Tom, a new team lead at Blue Yonder Airlines, says: "Claude's answers sound so confident that I assume they are correct."
questions.question: What is the most accurate response?

options.A: Accuracy problems mainly affected older models, so with a current model confident answers can usually be used as they are.
options.B: Claude sounds confident mainly when its answer comes from sources it has checked, so tone is a reasonable guide.
options.C: Confident wording is not evidence of accuracy; important claims still need checking.
options.D: If Claude were unsure about an answer, it would normally say so or decline, so a confident answer can generally be trusted.

questions.explanation: Language models produce fluent text whether or not the content is correct. Evaluate claims on their evidence, not on how assured they sound, and scale the checking to how much the output matters.

why_incorrect.A: All language models can make mistakes; newer models reduce but do not eliminate them.
why_incorrect.B: Confidence of tone is a writing style, not a signal that verification has happened.
why_incorrect.D: Claude can express uncertainty, but it does not reliably flag every answer that might be wrong.

questions.scenario: Claude drafted a market overview for Litware Publishing that includes the line "According to a 2025 Harrow Institute study, 64% of readers prefer audio formats." Nobody on the team has heard of the study.
questions.question: What should the team do?

options.A: Keep it, because a precise percentage, a year and a named institute are details that are unlikely to have been made up.
options.B: Change "64%" to "most readers" so the claim is less precise, which reduces the risk if the figure turns out to be slightly off.
options.C: Ask Claude whether the Harrow Institute study is real, and keep the statistic in the overview if Claude confirms it.
options.D: Treat it as unverified, search for the study independently, and remove it if no reliable source turns up.

questions.explanation: Unfamiliar studies, precise statistics and named experts are classic places where hallucinations appear. Verify them independently before use; if the source cannot be found, the claim should not appear in published material.

why_incorrect.A: Specific-looking details are a common feature of fabricated citations; specificity is not proof.
why_incorrect.B: Softening the number still attributes a claim to a source that may not exist.
why_incorrect.C: Claude may repeat the claim; independent verification is needed for a statistic that will be published.

questions.scenario: Claude produced a 15-page onboarding guide for Acme Logistics' new depot managers from three uploaded policy documents.
questions.question: Which TWO signals should prompt a closer check for inconsistency or fabrication?

options.A: The guide gives two different overtime approval limits in different sections.
options.B: The guide is written in plain English rather than the formal language of the policies, so some wording differs from the originals.
options.C: The guide repeats the company name several times.
options.D: The guide cites a "Policy 7.4" that does not appear in any of the uploaded documents.
options.E: The guide uses headings, numbered steps and bullet lists, which suggests Claude restructured the source material rather than quoting it.

questions.explanation: Internal contradictions and references to material not present in the sources are strong indicators that something has gone wrong. Both should be traced back to the uploaded documents before the guide is distributed.

why_incorrect.B: Plain language is often a requested style and is not a warning sign by itself.
why_incorrect.C: Repeating a company name is not an accuracy signal.
why_incorrect.E: Formatting is normal and does not indicate a factual problem.

questions.scenario: Graphic Design Institute's admissions office asks Claude to draft profiles of "a typical successful applicant" for marketing. Every draft describes applicants from the same narrow background and age range, though the institute's actual intake is diverse.
questions.question: What is the best interpretation and response?

options.A: The drafts are probably accurate, because Claude has been trained on very large amounts of data about students and education.
options.B: Stop using AI for any marketing content, since bias in outputs means the tool cannot be used responsibly in admissions.
options.C: The drafts may reflect stereotypes; give Claude real intake data, ask for varied profiles, and review them before use.
options.D: The issue is purely stylistic; ask for more colourful language.

questions.explanation: Model outputs can reproduce stereotypes present in training data, especially when asked for a "typical" person. Ground the task in real data, ask for diversity explicitly, and include a human review focused on fairness and representation.

why_incorrect.A: Large training data can still contain skewed patterns; it does not guarantee representative output.
why_incorrect.B: Bias can be reduced with grounding, explicit instructions and review; abandoning the tool is not the only option.
why_incorrect.D: Language style does not address who is being represented.

questions.scenario: Claude summarised a long email thread for Haruto at Margie's Travel. The summary says the client approved the itinerary on Tuesday, but a later email in the thread shows the client withdrew approval on Thursday.
questions.question: What kind of error is this, and how should Haruto prevent it next time?

options.A: A formatting problem; ask for the summary as a table with one row per email so that nothing in the thread is overlooked.
options.B: A wording error; ask Claude to proofread the summary carefully and correct any mistakes in the dates it mentions.
options.C: A later reversal was missed; ask Claude to track decisions in date order and flag any that were changed.
options.D: A tool failure that cannot be avoided, so stop summarising threads.

questions.explanation: Summaries of evolving conversations can capture an earlier state and miss later reversals. Asking for a dated decision log, with the latest status and any changes highlighted, makes such inconsistencies visible.

why_incorrect.A: A table could repeat the same mistake; the issue is how decisions over time are captured.
why_incorrect.B: The problem is factual and temporal, not orthographic.
why_incorrect.D: Asking for a chronological decision log with reversals is a practical fix; the task does not need to be abandoned.

questions.scenario: A trainer at Adatum Insurance is explaining to new staff what a "hallucination" means in the context of Claude.
questions.question: Which definition is most accurate?

options.A: Content presented as fact that the sources or reality do not support, such as an invented quote or reference.
options.B: Any content Claude invents, including the characters and events it writes when asked for a short story.
options.C: A response in which Claude says it is unsure or does not have enough information to answer.
options.D: An answer that is much longer or more detailed than the question required.

questions.explanation: A hallucination is unsupported content presented as fact. Knowing this helps staff focus checks on claims, names, numbers and references, which is where fabrication causes harm.

why_incorrect.B: Invented content in fiction is requested, not a factual error.
why_incorrect.C: Stating uncertainty is the honest alternative to hallucinating, not an example of it.
why_incorrect.D: Length is a style issue, not a hallucination.

questions.scenario: Claude answered a question for Fatima, a compliance assistant at Woodgrove Bank, using an uploaded 80-page internal procedures manual.
questions.question: Which instruction best supports fast fact-checking of the answer?

options.A: Ask Claude to add a confidence percentage to each statement, so she knows which parts to check most carefully.
options.B: Ask Claude to back each statement with a direct quote from the manual and the section heading it comes from.
options.C: Ask Claude to keep the answer to a few sentences, so there is less text for her to check against the 80-page manual.
options.D: Ask Claude to answer from general banking knowledge instead.

questions.explanation: Grounding answers in direct quotes with locations lets a reviewer check each claim in seconds. It also discourages statements that the source does not support, because each one must be tied to text.

why_incorrect.A: A self-reported percentage is not evidence and cannot be checked against the manual.
why_incorrect.C: Brevity does not help her locate the supporting text.
why_incorrect.D: General knowledge is harder to verify and may not match the organisation's own procedures.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's marketing team will publish a blog post drafted with Claude that includes product specifications, a customer quote and an industry growth figure.
questions.question: Which THREE validation steps are appropriate before publishing?

options.A: Ask Claude to rewrite the post so each claim is phrased more cautiously, using words like "around" and "reportedly" instead of specifics.
options.B: Run the post through a grammar and style checker as the final validation step before it goes to the web team.
options.C: Confirm product specifications against the official product documentation.
options.D: Trace the growth figure to its original publisher and check the date and definition.
options.E: Confirm the customer quote with the customer or the signed testimonial record.

questions.explanation: Each type of claim has a natural primary source: product docs for specifications, the person quoted for quotations, and the original publisher for statistics. Validation means checking claims at the source, not adjusting wording.

why_incorrect.A: Vaguer wording does not verify anything and may still mislead readers.
why_incorrect.B: A grammar checker improves language but does not confirm facts.

questions.scenario: Jonas, an analyst at Trey Research, used Claude's research feature to prepare a briefing on a regulatory consultation. The report includes citations to several web pages.
questions.question: What is the best way to use the citations when fact-checking?

options.A: Rely on the citations as they are, since research is designed to read each page and cite what supports the claim.
options.B: Count the citations per section; sections with more independent sources can be trusted and need no further checking.
options.C: Check that each citation link opens and comes from a reputable site, then accept the claims it supports.
options.D: Open the cited pages for the key claims and confirm each page actually says what is attributed to it.

questions.explanation: Citations make verification possible but are not verification in themselves. Spot-check that the cited source really supports the claim, focusing on the claims that matter most to the decision.

why_incorrect.A: Research can misread or over-generalise sources; citations exist so you can check.
why_incorrect.B: Volume of citations does not show that each claim is correctly supported.
why_incorrect.C: A working link on a reputable site does not confirm that the page supports the specific claim attributed to it.

questions.scenario: Alpine Ski House's analytics lead wants a lightweight, repeatable fact-checking routine for monthly performance reports drafted with Claude from uploaded booking data.
questions.question: Which routine is most effective?

options.A: Skim the report each month and check it thoroughly when a reader raises a concern, since errors are rare.
options.B: Ask Claude to grade its own report from 1 to 10 each month and publish if it scores 8 or higher.
options.C: Use a different model each month, so that any systematic mistakes from one model are caught by the next.
options.D: A fixed checklist: reconcile headline figures to source data, check comparisons to last month, and get a second reviewer for decision-driving claims.

questions.explanation: Good validation is systematic and proportionate: reconcile key figures to source data, check comparisons, and add human review where decisions depend on the output. A written routine makes the checks consistent month to month.

why_incorrect.A: Reactive checking lets errors reach decision-makers first, and a skim does not reconcile figures to the source.
why_incorrect.B: Self-grading is not independent and the score is not tied to specific checks.
why_incorrect.C: Changing models adds variation without verifying the numbers.

questions.scenario: Claude gave Mariam at Fourth Coffee an answer about local food-hygiene inspection frequency without saying where the information came from. She needs to rely on it for a store-opening plan.
questions.question: What should she do first?

options.A: Use the answer as given, since food-hygiene inspection rules are broadly standardised and an unsourced summary is usually enough.
options.B: Ask Claude to restate the answer in more formal, precise language so it can be quoted directly in the opening plan.
options.C: Check the official authority's website, or ask Claude to find and cite the official source, then confirm it.
options.D: Ask an experienced colleague whether the inspection frequency sounds about right, and proceed if they agree.

questions.explanation: For requirements that carry consequences, verify against an authoritative primary source. Claude can help find and cite it, but the final check is against the official publication.

why_incorrect.A: Requirements vary by location and over time, so an unsourced general answer is risky.
why_incorrect.B: Rewording does not add a source or confirm the requirement.
why_incorrect.D: An opinion that it "sounds right" is weaker than checking the official source.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery uses Claude for several tasks: brainstorming social media hashtags, drafting internal meeting agendas, summarising staff survey comments, and drafting the allergen statement printed on product labels.
questions.question: Which output most clearly requires formal expert review before use?

options.A: The hashtag brainstorm, because posts are public and any wording could be seen by customers.
options.B: A first-pass summary of survey comments for the team to discuss.
options.C: The allergen statement for product labels.
options.D: The internal meeting agenda, because it sets the decisions the leadership team will discuss.

questions.explanation: Review effort should scale with impact. Content that affects health, legal compliance or public safety, such as allergen labelling, needs expert sign-off. Low-stakes internal drafts need only a sensible read-through.

why_incorrect.A: Hashtags are low-risk and easy to adjust; a quick read is enough.
why_incorrect.B: Internal discussion material deserves a sense check, but errors are lower-stakes than safety-critical label content.
why_incorrect.D: An agenda is internal and easily corrected in the meeting itself.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Clinics is piloting Claude to help administrative staff draft replies to patient enquiries about appointments, billing and general clinic information.
questions.question: Which TWO situations should always be routed to a qualified human before anything is sent?

options.A: A request for the clinic's parking information and opening hours over the holiday period.
options.B: A thank-you note from a patient.
options.C: A request to move a routine follow-up appointment to the following week because the patient will be travelling.
options.D: A message describing new chest pain and asking whether to come in.
options.E: A billing dispute where the patient says they are being charged for a procedure they did not have.

questions.explanation: Human review is essential where an error could cause harm or significant financial or legal consequences: clinical symptoms and contested charges are clear examples. Low-risk informational replies can follow a lighter process.

why_incorrect.A: Factual, low-risk information can follow a lighter review process.
why_incorrect.B: A courtesy acknowledgement carries little risk.
why_incorrect.C: Routine scheduling is low risk and can follow a standard, lighter check.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's content team produces about 200 destination blurbs a month with Claude. Reviewing every blurb in depth takes too long, but errors have occasionally reached the website.
questions.question: What review approach balances effort and risk best?

options.A: Check all blurbs for high-risk content such as visa or safety statements, and spot-check a sample of the rest.
options.B: Ask Claude to review and correct its own blurbs before publishing, replacing the human review step with an automated check.
options.C: Stop reviewing, since errors are rare and the time saved can be spent on producing more destination content each month.
options.D: Review every blurb in full depth, regardless of its content, because any error on the website is equally damaging.

questions.explanation: Risk-based review targets human attention where errors matter most, with sampling to monitor overall quality. Feedback from sampling tells the team when to tighten or relax checks.

why_incorrect.B: Self-review can help but is not an independent check on high-risk claims.
why_incorrect.C: Errors have already reached the website, so removing review increases risk.
why_incorrect.D: Uniform deep review is the cost the team cannot sustain, and it spends effort on low-risk text.

questions.scenario: A manager at Datum Corp asks when it is acceptable to use a Claude draft without further checking.
questions.question: Which guideline is most sensible?

options.A: Whenever the draft is long and detailed, since detail shows that Claude has considered the topic thoroughly.
options.B: Whenever a colleague has already used a similar Claude draft for the same kind of task without problems.
options.C: When the content is low-stakes, easy to correct, and you can judge its quality yourself.
options.D: Whenever the draft was produced by the most capable model available on the company's plan.

questions.explanation: The need for review depends on stakes, reversibility and your ability to judge the content. Low-risk, easily corrected work can be used with a light read; consequential output needs proportionate verification.

why_incorrect.A: Length and detail do not indicate accuracy.
why_incorrect.B: Past success on similar drafts says nothing about whether this draft's content is correct.
why_incorrect.D: Any model can make errors; capability does not remove the need for review on important work.

questions.scenario: Claude drafted a technical incident summary for Relecloud's engineering team. The same incident must now be explained to customers in a status update.
questions.question: What is the best way to adapt the content?

options.A: Ask Claude to rewrite it for customers: plain language, impact on them, what was done, and what happens next.
options.B: Send the engineering summary unchanged, because customers appreciate full technical transparency about what went wrong.
options.C: Translate the summary into formal legal language to be safe.
options.D: Shorten the engineering summary by about half, removing the most technical paragraphs and keeping the rest as it is.

questions.explanation: Adapting for an audience means changing vocabulary, emphasis and level of detail, not just length. Tell Claude who the reader is and what they need to know, and remove internal details that do not serve them.

why_incorrect.B: Internal jargon and system names confuse customers and may expose unnecessary internal detail.
why_incorrect.C: Legal register does not make the update clearer or more useful to customers.
why_incorrect.D: Mechanical cutting keeps the wrong vocabulary and may drop the information customers need.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Events asked Claude for two versions of a sponsorship proposal: one emphasising brand visibility, one emphasising lead generation. The sales director must pick one for a technology sponsor.
questions.question: What is the most useful way to use Claude in comparing them?

options.A: Ask Claude to compare both versions against the sponsor's stated goals, listing strengths, gaps and edits for each.
options.B: Merge both versions in full so nothing is lost.
options.C: Ask Claude which version it prefers overall, since it wrote both and is well placed to judge which one is stronger.
options.D: Pick the longer version, because a sponsor making a significant investment will expect more detail.

questions.explanation: Comparison is most useful when anchored to explicit criteria, here the sponsor's goals. Claude can structure the comparison, but the decision rests on fit with audience needs.

why_incorrect.B: Combining everything produces an unfocused proposal that serves neither goal well.
why_incorrect.C: Preference without criteria does not help the director decide for this sponsor.
why_incorrect.D: Length does not indicate fit with the sponsor's priorities.

questions.scenario: Bellows College needs Claude's draft research summary on student well-being adapted for three audiences: the governing board, students, and the student-services team.
questions.question: Which TWO adaptations are appropriate?

options.A: For the three audiences: send one shared draft so that each group receives a consistent message.
options.B: For students: plain, supportive language focused on what changes for them and where to get help.
options.C: For the board: a one-page summary leading with decisions needed, risks and resource implications.
options.D: For students: include the full statistical appendix so they can see the methodology.
options.E: For the student-services team: remove the recommendations so staff can form their own view of the findings.

questions.explanation: The same facts should be framed differently for each audience: decisions and risks for leaders, practical meaning and support for affected people, and actionable detail for operational teams.

why_incorrect.A: Consistent facts matter, but identical wording ignores very different needs.
why_incorrect.D: Most students need the practical implications, not detailed statistics; the appendix can be linked for those who want it.
why_incorrect.E: Operational teams need recommendations to act on; removing them defeats the purpose.

questions.scenario: Claude rewrote a dense policy for Humongous Insurance's frontline staff in simpler language. In simplifying, it turned "may, subject to manager approval" into "can".
questions.question: What is the main risk, and what should the editor do?

options.A: There is little risk, because plain language is known to improve compliance among frontline staff.
options.B: The main risk is that the text is now too short to be taken seriously; ask Claude to expand it again.
options.C: Simplifying changed the meaning; check conditions and permissions survive, and tell Claude to keep such qualifiers.
options.D: The main risk is tone; ask Claude to make the simplified policy sound friendlier and more supportive.

questions.explanation: When adapting text for a new audience, check that meaning-carrying words such as conditions, exceptions and obligations survive. Telling Claude which qualifiers must be preserved prevents simplifications that change the rule.

why_incorrect.A: Plain language helps only if the meaning stays the same; here a condition was lost.
why_incorrect.B: Length is not the issue; a key condition was dropped.
why_incorrect.D: Tone does not fix the missing approval requirement.

questions.scenario: Nadia at Fabrikam Retail wants Claude to build a reusable one-page store-visit checklist that her team will edit and refer to over several weeks.
questions.question: Which output format fits best?

options.A: A screenshot of the chat.
options.B: A short inline chat reply, so the checklist stays in the conversation flow where the team already discusses visits.
options.C: An artifact, which sits beside the chat and can be revisited, edited and shared.
options.D: A long, unstructured paragraph covering every item, so that nothing is lost when people copy it into emails.

questions.explanation: Artifacts suit substantial, self-contained content that people will reuse or edit, such as documents, checklists or small tools. Quick answers and conversational explanations usually stay inline.

why_incorrect.A: A screenshot cannot be edited and is awkward to reuse.
why_incorrect.B: Inline replies are good for quick answers, but substantial content that will be reused and edited fits an artifact better.
why_incorrect.D: A checklist needs structure; an unstructured paragraph is harder to use.

questions.scenario: A data coordinator at Proseware Education asks Claude to extract course codes, titles, credit values and prerequisites from 40 pages of course descriptions. The results will be imported into a spreadsheet.
questions.question: Which output format should she request?

options.A: A flexible list where each course is described in whatever layout best fits its information.
options.B: A slide outline with one course per slide.
options.C: A narrative summary of each course in short paragraphs, so that prerequisites and context are explained clearly.
options.D: A table or CSV with fixed column names, one row per course, and an explicit value for missing fields.

questions.explanation: When output feeds another tool, ask for a defined structure with fixed fields and a rule for missing data. This makes the result machine-friendly and makes gaps visible.

why_incorrect.A: Inconsistent layouts break the import and hide missing values.
why_incorrect.B: Slides are a presentation format, not a data-import format.
why_incorrect.C: Paragraphs are hard to import and make it easy to miss a field.

questions.scenario: Datum Corp's chief of staff asks Claude to turn 60 pages of department updates into material for a 30-minute executive meeting.
questions.question: Which TWO curation choices are most helpful?

options.A: Group updates by strategic priority rather than by department, so executives can see progress against goals.
options.B: Include every update verbatim, organised by department, so executives can see each team's full report and nothing is lost in curation.
options.C: Lead with decisions required and top risks, and move routine status details into an appendix.
options.D: Remove most numbers and metrics to keep the material short and readable for the 30-minute meeting.
options.E: Order the updates by department, with each department's highlights at the top of its section.

questions.explanation: Curating means selecting and organising information for the reader's purpose: decisions and risks first, structure aligned with goals, and supporting detail available but not in the way.

why_incorrect.B: Executives cannot absorb 60 pages in 30 minutes; curation is the point of the task.
why_incorrect.D: Key metrics are often what executives need; stripping numbers loses important evidence.
why_incorrect.E: Department order mirrors the organisation chart, not the decisions and priorities executives need to focus on.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel's operations manager wants a simple interactive tool that lets agents enter trip length and party size and see an estimated insurance premium band. She has no coding skills.
questions.question: Which approach in the Claude app is most suitable?

options.A: Ask Claude to describe the band rules clearly in prose and have agents work out the premium band by hand each time.
options.B: Ask Claude to build an interactive artifact with the inputs and her band rules, test it on known cases, then share it.
options.C: Ask Claude to create the premium bands itself using typical industry averages, so she does not need to supply the rules.
options.D: Paste the rules into a long inline reply and ask agents to search it each time.

questions.explanation: Artifacts can be small interactive tools, not only documents. When the rules come from the business and are tested against known cases, a non-technical user can create a useful internal helper.

why_incorrect.A: This works but misses the request; an interactive artifact meets it directly without coding.
why_incorrect.C: Pricing rules must come from the business; invented bands would be unreliable.
why_incorrect.D: A long inline reply is hard to use repeatedly compared with a dedicated tool.

questions.scenario: Every week, Oliver at Acme Logistics asks Claude questions about the same carrier contracts, rate cards and escalation procedures. He re-uploads the same five files and re-explains his role each time.
questions.question: Which Claude feature best fits this recurring work?

options.A: A Project with the five files in its knowledge and instructions describing his role and preferred style.
options.B: A new standalone chat each week with the files re-attached.
options.C: The research feature, so Claude can search for and gather the latest versions of his contracts each time he asks a question.
options.D: A shared artifact that combines the five files into one reference document.

questions.explanation: Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own knowledge base and instructions that apply to every chat in the project. They suit recurring work on the same materials.

why_incorrect.B: This is exactly the repetitive set-up he wants to avoid; nothing persists between standalone chats by design.
why_incorrect.C: His contracts are internal documents, not web content; research is for multi-source investigation, often on the web.
why_incorrect.D: Artifacts are outputs Claude creates, not a store of reference documents and instructions for future chats.

questions.scenario: Selin, a strategy analyst at Woodgrove Bank, needs a well-sourced overview of how five competitor banks have changed their mobile app features over the past year, drawing on many public sources.
questions.question: Which Claude capability is the best fit?

options.A: A single web search in an ordinary chat, asking Claude to list each competitor's mobile app changes.
options.B: An artifact that Claude builds from its training data alone, structured as a competitor-by-feature comparison table.
options.C: Research, which runs multiple linked searches, follows leads and produces a cited report.
options.D: A Project containing last year's internal strategy deck.

questions.explanation: Research is designed for multi-step investigation: it runs a series of searches, decides what to look at next and cites its sources. Simple web search is better for quick factual lookups.

why_incorrect.A: A single quick search suits simple factual lookups; this question needs many searches across sources.
why_incorrect.B: Training data has a cutoff and lacks sources; the task needs current, cited information.
why_incorrect.D: An old internal deck cannot provide the past year's external changes.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's regional manager has four tasks this week: (1) a quick check of today's opening hours for a supplier's office, (2) an ongoing workspace for monthly store-performance reviews using the same templates, (3) a shareable interactive staff rota planner, and (4) a one-off question about how to phrase a thank-you note.
questions.question: Which TWO feature matches are correct?

options.A: Task 2: a Project holding the templates and review instructions.
options.B: Task 2: a separate standalone chat each month, re-attaching the templates, so each month's review starts clean.
options.C: Task 3: an artifact the manager can refine and share.
options.D: Task 4: a new Project with uploaded etiquette guides.
options.E: Task 1: the research feature, so that the supplier's opening hours are checked across several sources and cited.

questions.explanation: Match features to the shape of the work: chat (with web search if needed) for quick one-off questions, Projects for recurring work on shared materials, artifacts for standalone outputs to reuse or share, and research for deep multi-source investigation.

why_incorrect.B: Recurring work on the same templates benefits from a Project rather than repeating the set-up each time.
why_incorrect.D: A one-off question is well served by an ordinary chat; a Project adds unnecessary set-up.
why_incorrect.E: Research takes longer and uses more of the usage allowance; a quick web search fits a simple fact lookup.

questions.scenario: A new user at Litware Publishing asks how Skills differ from Projects in the Claude apps.
questions.question: Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Skills and Projects are two names for the same capability: a place to store reusable instructions and files for later chats.
options.B: Skills are packaged instructions and resources Claude loads when relevant; Projects are workspaces with chats, knowledge and instructions.
options.C: Projects are loaded automatically into any chat whenever their content seems relevant; Skills are folders of uploaded reference files.
options.D: Skills are a developer feature used through the API and Claude Code, not something users add in the Claude apps.

questions.explanation: Skills give Claude procedural know-how (for example, how to produce a report in a house format) and load only when relevant. Projects group related chats with shared knowledge and instructions. They complement each other.

why_incorrect.A: They serve different purposes: one packages reusable procedures, the other organises work and context.
why_incorrect.C: That describes how Skills are loaded; Project knowledge applies to chats inside that Project.
why_incorrect.D: Skills are available in the Claude apps across plans, not just for developers.

questions.scenario: A team lead at Contoso Health is introducing Claude's model families to colleagues.
questions.question: Which description of the families is most accurate?

options.A: Haiku is fastest and lowest-cost, Sonnet balances speed and intelligence, Opus targets complex work.
options.B: The three families differ mainly in knowledge cut-off date, with Opus the most recent and Haiku the oldest.
options.C: Haiku is specialised for images, Sonnet for written text and Opus for audio and voice tasks.
options.D: Opus is the fastest family because it is the largest, while Haiku is slower but uses the least capacity.

questions.explanation: Claude's families form a capability ladder. Haiku prioritises speed and cost, Sonnet offers the best balance for many tasks, and Opus targets the hardest reasoning and long-running work (as of 2026-10-24).

why_incorrect.B: The families have different capability, speed and cost profiles; the names do not indicate training dates.
why_incorrect.C: The families differ in capability, speed and cost, not in which single input type they handle.
why_incorrect.D: Larger, more capable models are generally slower, not faster.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's product team wants to tag 2,000 short app-store reviews by theme (pricing, bugs, usability) each week. Tags must be consistent, and the work is simple and repetitive.
questions.question: Which model family is the most natural starting point?

options.A: Whichever model was released most recently, regardless of the task.
options.B: No model; tagging cannot be done by language models.
options.C: Opus, because consistency of tags matters, and the most capable model should be used whenever consistency is a requirement.
options.D: Haiku, because the task is simple, high-volume and speed-sensitive; check a sample for accuracy.

questions.explanation: Simple, repetitive tasks such as classification often run well on the fastest family. Start there, check quality on a sample, and move up only if accuracy falls short.

why_incorrect.A: Release date does not determine the best fit for a specific workload.
why_incorrect.B: Classification and tagging are well-suited tasks for language models.
why_incorrect.C: Using the most capable model for simple classification spends more capacity than the task needs.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending's strategy director needs Claude to work through a 90-page market study, reconcile conflicting figures across chapters, and build a nuanced investment memo with explicit assumptions.
questions.question: Which model choice is most appropriate?

options.A: Split the study into one-page pieces and use a different model for each.
options.B: Haiku, because it is the fastest family and the director wants the memo quickly for the next investment committee.
options.C: Any current model, because they share a long context window and so handle long documents equally well.
options.D: An Opus-class model, because deep reasoning across a long document matters more here than speed.

questions.explanation: Complex, high-stakes reasoning over long material is where the most capable families earn their extra time and usage. Reserve them for tasks where quality is the deciding factor.

why_incorrect.A: Fragmenting the document makes reconciling cross-chapter conflicts harder, not easier.
why_incorrect.B: Speed is less important here than careful reasoning; the fastest family is not tuned for this depth of work.
why_incorrect.C: A long context window lets a model read the document, but models still differ in reasoning depth; complex synthesis benefits from a more capable family.

questions.scenario: A trainer at Bellows College is correcting common misconceptions about Claude's model families.
questions.question: Which TWO statements are accurate?

options.A: A more capable model is usually slower and uses more of the usage allowance than a smaller one on the same task.
options.B: Smaller families can read much shorter documents, so long documents need the largest family.
options.C: Smaller models are reliable enough on simple tasks that their outputs do not need checking, unlike outputs from larger models.
options.D: The newest and largest model gives the best value for most tasks, because it needs fewer follow-up messages.
options.E: The best model depends on the task; a balanced model such as Sonnet is a sensible default for many everyday tasks.

questions.explanation: Model choice is a trade-off among capability, speed and usage. The right choice depends on the task, and a balanced family is a reasonable default for many everyday tasks.

why_incorrect.B: Current families all have long context windows; they differ mainly in capability, speed and cost, not in how much they can read.
why_incorrect.C: All models can make mistakes; outputs still need appropriate checking.
why_incorrect.D: Larger models are slower and use more of the allowance; for many everyday tasks a balanced model is enough.

questions.scenario: Ravi at VanArsdel Foods hits his plan's usage limit by mid-week. Most of his chats are short email rewrites and quick formatting fixes, all done on the most capable model.
questions.question: What change would most help him stay within his limits without hurting quality?

options.A: Start each task in a fresh chat with his reference files re-uploaded, so Claude has a clean context.
options.B: Keep using the most capable model for everything but write longer, more detailed prompts so fewer follow-ups are needed.
options.C: Use a lighter model for routine rewrites and formatting, and keep the most capable one for complex analysis.
options.D: Use the research feature for each rewrite, since it gathers more context and so reduces the number of messages he sends.

questions.explanation: Model choice affects how quickly usage limits are reached. Matching lighter models to routine tasks and reserving the most capable model for demanding work preserves both quality and capacity.

why_incorrect.A: Repeatedly attaching large files consumes more of the allowance.
why_incorrect.B: Longer prompts on the heaviest model use more of the allowance, not less.
why_incorrect.D: Research uses limits faster and adds nothing to a simple rewrite.

questions.scenario: Blue Yonder Airlines' customer-insights team needs a first draft of 30 internal survey invitation variations within the hour. Quality needs are moderate, and a human will polish the final choice.
questions.question: Which trade-off is most sensible?

options.A: Prioritise speed with a faster model, then have the editor refine the chosen variations.
options.B: Use the most capable model, because wording affects response rates and a stronger first draft saves editing.
options.C: Ask for five variations now and have the team write the remaining 25 by adapting those themselves.
options.D: Use the research feature so each variation is grounded in best practice on survey response rates.

questions.explanation: When deadlines are tight, quality needs are moderate and a human will refine the output, a faster model is the efficient choice.

why_incorrect.B: Depth matters less than speed here; quality needs are moderate and the human editor will polish the result anyway.
why_incorrect.C: The team needs 30 options within the hour; shifting most of the writing to people defeats the purpose.
why_incorrect.D: Research is slow and uses more allowance; it is not needed to generate short copy variations against a tight deadline.

questions.scenario: Adatum Insurance is setting team guidance on model choice in the Claude apps for three recurring tasks: summarising daily news clippings, drafting complex claims-dispute analyses, and reformatting tables.
questions.question: Which TWO guidelines are sound?

options.A: Use the most capable model for the three tasks, so that quality is consistent and nobody has to make model decisions day to day.
options.B: Choose the model based on which one the team lead prefers.
options.C: Use the lightest model for everything, because staying within usage limits matters more than small quality differences on any task.
options.D: Use the most capable model for complex claims-dispute analyses, where reasoning quality matters most.
options.E: Pilot each task on a lighter model, compare a few outputs with a stronger model, and step up only where quality differs meaningfully.

questions.explanation: Good model guidance is task-based and evidence-based: test lighter options, step up where quality requires it, and reserve the most capable models for complex work.

why_incorrect.A: A blanket rule wastes capacity on simple tasks such as reformatting tables.
why_incorrect.B: Preference is not a substitute for testing fit against task requirements.
why_incorrect.C: Complex analyses can suffer on the lightest model; quality needs differ by task.

questions.scenario: Lena at Southridge Video switched from a balanced model to a lighter one to stretch her usage. Short rewrites are fine, but her multi-step budget variance explanations now skip steps and miss interactions between line items.
questions.question: What should she do?

options.A: Switch every task, including short rewrites, back to the most capable model available.
options.B: Use the more capable model for variance analyses and the lighter model for short rewrites.
options.C: Keep the lighter model for everything and add "think carefully, step by step" to the variance prompts to recover the quality.
options.D: Stop doing variance analyses with Claude altogether.

questions.explanation: Model choice can be made per task. When a lighter model degrades quality on complex reasoning, move that task back to a more capable model while keeping simpler tasks on the efficient option.

why_incorrect.A: Short rewrites are working fine; moving them to the heaviest model spends usage unnecessarily.
why_incorrect.C: Asking for careful reasoning may help a little, but the evidence shows the lighter model struggles with this multi-step task; moving it to a more capable model is the reliable fix.
why_incorrect.D: The task worked before on a more capable model; the issue is the model choice, not the use case.

questions.scenario: After a very long chat about a product launch plan, Grace at Fabrikam Retail notices Claude has started forgetting decisions made near the beginning and is giving less focused answers.
questions.question: What is the most effective step?

options.A: Stay in the same chat and restate the earlier decisions in each new message so Claude keeps them in view.
options.B: Delete her earliest messages so the chat becomes shorter.
options.C: Switch the chat to a lighter model, which handles long conversations more efficiently and keeps answers focused.
options.D: Ask Claude for a summary of agreed decisions and open items, check it, and continue in a new chat from that summary.

questions.explanation: Very long conversations can lose focus and use more of the usage allowance. A checked summary carried into a fresh chat keeps the important context while giving Claude a clean starting point.

why_incorrect.A: Repeating material makes the conversation even longer, which worsens the problem.
why_incorrect.B: The early decisions are what she needs; removing them loses that context entirely.
why_incorrect.C: A lighter model does not restore lost focus from a very long conversation.

questions.scenario: Omar at Trey Research works across several client Projects. He wants Claude to remember his general writing preferences everywhere, but he does not want details from one client Project to appear in another.
questions.question: Which understanding of memory is correct?

options.A: Memory is one shared pool, so anything discussed in one client Project is available in every other Project's chats.
options.B: Each Project has its own memory that other Projects do not use; account memory can hold general preferences.
options.C: Memory is not available inside Projects, so he would need to restate his writing preferences in every Project chat.
options.D: To keep clients separate, he must create a separate Claude account per client.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, memory in the Claude apps is scoped: each Project keeps its own memory, and chats inside a Project use that Project's memory plus account-level memory, not other Projects' memory. A Project can also be set to ignore account memory.

why_incorrect.A: Project memory is kept separate per Project rather than pooled across Projects.
why_incorrect.C: Projects have their own memory; it is scoped to the Project.
why_incorrect.D: Project-scoped memory already separates Projects, and a Project can also be set not to use account memory.

questions.scenario: Hannah at Proseware Education wants a quick brainstorm about a personal topic and does not want it saved to Claude's memory or chat history.
questions.question: Which option achieves this?

options.A: Start an incognito chat, which is not saved to memory or chat history.
options.B: Open Claude in her browser's private window, so the conversation is not stored once the window closes.
options.C: Start the chat inside a new Project, since chats in a Project are kept out of her account memory and history.
options.D: Turn memory off for that chat before sending the first message.
options.E: Ask Claude at the end to forget everything discussed, which removes the chat from memory and from her history.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, incognito chats are not saved to memory or chat history, so they meet both of Hannah's requirements. Memory can also be switched off for a single chat before the first message is sent, but that chat stays in chat history and can still be found when Claude searches past chats, so it does not keep the brainstorm out of history. (Note: on Team and Enterprise plans, incognito chats can still be subject to organisation retention and export policies.)

why_incorrect.B: A private browser window affects what the browser stores locally, not what is saved to her Claude account.
why_incorrect.C: Project chats appear in chat history and use the Project's own memory; a Project does not make a chat private.
why_incorrect.D: Turning memory off for one chat keeps it out of memory, but the chat still stays in her chat history.
why_incorrect.E: She can ask Claude to forget specific memories, but this does not stop the chat being saved in history; incognito does.

questions.scenario: Datum Corp's operations team uses one Project for a nine-month process-improvement programme. Key decisions are scattered across dozens of chats, and new team members get inconsistent answers about what was decided.
