questions.question: What is the best way to persist decisions so every chat in the Project uses them?

options.A: Paste the full text of the key past chats into the Project instructions so every new chat starts with the history.
options.B: Ask each team member to tell Claude the decisions they know about, so they are stored in their own account memory.
options.C: Keep a concise, dated decision log in the Project knowledge and update it as decisions are made.
options.D: Continue the programme in one long-running chat so the full discussion history stays in a single place.

questions.explanation: Project knowledge is available to every chat in the Project, so a curated decision log is a reliable way to persist important context. It is also readable by people, which helps onboarding and governance. Memory, including a Project's own memory, is generated automatically from chats rather than curated, so it cannot be reviewed, dated and corrected like a shared decision log, and each member's account memory is personal to them.

why_incorrect.A: Instructions should be concise guidance; dumping chat transcripts there adds noise and bulk.
why_incorrect.B: Account memory is personal to each member, so new joiners do not get it, and it is not a reviewed, dated record anyone can read.
why_incorrect.D: One very long chat degrades focus, uses more of the allowance and is hard for new members to navigate.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail's store-operations lead has 25 pages of interview notes from store managers about a new stock-counting process. She wants Claude's help turning them into requirements.
questions.question: Which request will produce the most useful starting point?

options.A: Ask Claude to write the full new process design straight away from the notes, so stakeholders have something concrete to react to.
options.B: Ask Claude to summarise the notes in one paragraph.
options.C: Ask Claude to extract distinct needs, group them by theme, mark must-have or nice-to-have with a quote, and list open questions.
options.D: Ask Claude to add requirements that store managers probably forgot, so that the list is as complete as possible from the start.

questions.explanation: Claude is effective at structuring qualitative input into candidate requirements. Asking for themes, priorities, source quotes and open questions keeps the analysis traceable and highlights where stakeholders still need to decide.

why_incorrect.A: Designing before requirements are agreed skips the analysis and hides gaps in the notes.
why_incorrect.B: A single paragraph loses the individual needs, priorities and evidence that requirements work depends on.
why_incorrect.D: Invented requirements are not grounded in stakeholder input and should be raised as questions, not asserted.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Clinics' operations director lists ten ideas for using Claude and asks Mateo, an analyst, to recommend which to pilot first.
questions.question: Which TWO criteria should carry the most weight when using Claude to evaluate the use cases?

options.A: The risk if Claude's output is wrong, and whether a practical human review step exists.
options.B: The value of the outcome (time saved or quality gained) relative to the effort to set up the use case.
options.C: Which ideas would remove the most staff roles.
options.D: Which ideas would make the most impressive demonstration for the board, since visible early wins build support for wider adoption.
options.E: Which ideas use the largest number of Claude features at once, since broad pilots reveal more about the tool's capabilities.

questions.explanation: Good first pilots combine clear value, reasonable effort and manageable risk with a workable review step. Claude can help score options against these criteria, but the criteria themselves should reflect business outcomes and risk.

why_incorrect.C: Use-case selection should focus on value and risk; framing pilots around headcount cuts also tends to undermine adoption and trust.
why_incorrect.D: Demo appeal does not reflect sustained value or manageable risk.
why_incorrect.E: Feature count is not a measure of value; simpler use cases often deliver more.

questions.scenario: Claude helped Alpine Ski House draft user stories for a new rental booking process. In review, the finance team says none of the stories cover deposits and refunds, which are critical for them.
questions.question: What most likely went wrong in the requirements analysis?

options.A: The inputs did not include finance stakeholders' needs, so the stories could only reflect the views provided.
options.B: The stories were written too briefly, so details such as deposits and refunds were cut out to save space.
options.C: Claude is cautious about financial topics, so it tends to leave payment-related requirements for people to write.
options.D: The model used was optimised for speed, so it skipped the less common parts of the booking process.

questions.explanation: Requirements generated with Claude are only as complete as the stakeholder input supplied. Before drafting, list the stakeholder groups and confirm each group's needs are represented, or ask Claude to identify perspectives that seem to be missing.

why_incorrect.B: Length does not explain a whole missing stakeholder perspective.
why_incorrect.C: Claude can write financial user stories; it simply was not given that stakeholder input.
why_incorrect.D: Missing coverage is caused by missing inputs, not by model speed.

questions.scenario: Datum Corp's legal operations team wants to "use Claude for contract review." Requirements discussions keep stalling because people mean different things by the phrase.
questions.question: What is the most productive way to use Claude to move the analysis forward?

options.A: Choose the broadest interpretation and ask Claude to design an end-to-end automated review of every contract, so nothing is left out.
options.B: Ask Claude to break "contract review" into concrete use cases (clause extraction, playbook deviation flags, business summaries) with inputs, outputs and review points.
options.C: Ask Claude for a definition of contract review from a dictionary.
options.D: Postpone the analysis until a vendor can provide a ready-made solution.

questions.explanation: Vague requests become workable once they are decomposed into concrete use cases with defined inputs, outputs and human checkpoints. Claude is useful for producing that breakdown so stakeholders can compare and choose.

why_incorrect.A: An undefined, all-encompassing scope increases risk and makes success hard to measure.
why_incorrect.C: A dictionary definition does not resolve which specific tasks the team needs.
why_incorrect.D: Delay does not clarify requirements; the team still needs to define what it wants.

questions.scenario: A business analyst at Margie's Travel asks how Claude can best support requirements work without replacing stakeholder conversations.
questions.question: Which description is most accurate?

options.A: Claude can run the requirements process end to end, with the analyst reviewing the final document.
options.B: Claude can organise notes, draft requirements and suggest gaps, while stakeholders confirm priorities and decide.
options.C: Claude can determine the real business requirements from general industry knowledge, so stakeholder interviews become optional.
options.D: Claude is best used after requirements are signed off, to turn them into polished documentation.

questions.explanation: Claude augments requirements analysis by structuring information and surfacing gaps. Ownership of priorities and decisions stays with the people accountable for the outcome.

why_incorrect.A: Claude augments the analyst's work; judgement, facilitation and decisions stay with people.
why_incorrect.C: Claude cannot know an organisation's needs unless they are provided; stakeholders remain the source.
why_incorrect.D: Claude is helpful during analysis, for example structuring interview notes and spotting gaps.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's logistics coordinator wants to reduce the time it takes to process distributor orders. She can describe each step of the current process in detail.
questions.question: How can Claude help most effectively at the start?

options.A: Ask Claude to guarantee a 50% time reduction.
options.B: Ask Claude to recommend new logistics software straight away, since a better tool is the fastest way to cut processing time.
options.C: Ask Claude to map the steps, find hand-offs, delays and duplication, and suggest options to test, stating assumptions.
options.D: Ask Claude to design a completely new order process from best practice, without describing the current one, to avoid bias.

questions.explanation: Process optimisation starts with an accurate picture of the current state. Claude can map steps, highlight likely bottlenecks and propose experiments, as long as assumptions are explicit and results are tested in practice.

why_incorrect.A: Claude cannot guarantee outcomes for a process it has only seen described; results need testing.
why_incorrect.B: Choosing tools comes after understanding where the bottlenecks are.
why_incorrect.D: Without the current process, Claude cannot identify where time is actually lost.

questions.scenario: Graphic Design Institute's head of operations is planning a move to a new student information system next year and wants Claude to help build the project plan.
questions.question: Which TWO uses of Claude are most appropriate?

options.A: Producing a plan from a generic project template, then adding the institute's details later.
options.B: Committing the institute to final go-live dates based on Claude's draft, so the vendor can begin scheduling work straight away.
options.C: Generating a checklist of questions to ask the vendor and internal teams to uncover hidden dependencies.
options.D: Drafting a phased plan with milestones, dependencies and risks based on the scope, dates and constraints she provides.
options.E: Approving the project budget on finance's behalf once Claude has estimated the costs from the vendor's price list.

questions.explanation: Claude is a strong planning partner: it drafts structured plans from provided context and surfaces questions that reveal risks. Commitments and approvals remain with the accountable people.

why_incorrect.A: A generic plan ignores the institute's own constraints, systems and calendar.
why_incorrect.B: Plans need validation by the people doing the work; Claude's draft dates are a starting point, not commitments.
why_incorrect.E: Budget approval is a human governance decision, not something to delegate to Claude.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's procurement team wants a comparison of three document e-signature vendors' published security certifications and pricing models, using information from the vendors' public websites.
questions.question: Which approach best combines Claude's capabilities with verification?

options.A: Ask Claude in an ordinary chat to list each vendor's certifications and pricing from what it already knows, to save time.
options.B: Rely on each vendor's own comparison sheet, since vendors know their products best.
options.C: Ask Claude to compare the vendors and choose one, so the procurement team can move straight to the paperwork.
options.D: Use research to gather and cite the vendors' published information, then confirm key claims with the vendors.

questions.explanation: Research tasks about third parties benefit from cited, current sources followed by targeted human confirmation, especially for claims that drive contractual or security decisions.

why_incorrect.A: Certifications change and recall may be outdated; current, cited sources are needed.
why_incorrect.B: Vendor comparison sheets are marketing; procurement decisions need claims confirmed, ideally with formal evidence.
why_incorrect.C: The decision and its accountability stay with the procurement team.

questions.scenario: Acme Logistics' planning team uses Claude to draft weekly driver schedules. A manager suggests asking Claude for the "optimal" schedule across 400 drivers with dozens of hard constraints and simply using whatever it produces.
questions.question: What is the most sensible approach?

options.A: Avoid Claude entirely for anything related to scheduling.
options.B: Ask Claude for the schedule several times and choose the version that looks most balanced, since repeated attempts reduce error.
options.C: Use Claude to clarify constraints, explain trade-offs and review exceptions, but generate or check the schedule with a tool that tests every constraint.
options.D: Accept Claude's schedule as optimal because language models are good at maths.

questions.explanation: Know where Claude fits in a process. It excels at language, structure and reasoning about trade-offs, but exhaustive constraint checking across hundreds of records needs a deterministic tool or explicit verification.

why_incorrect.A: Claude still adds value in clarifying constraints, explaining options and drafting communications.
why_incorrect.B: Picking by appearance does not verify that hard constraints are met.
why_incorrect.D: Large constraint-satisfaction problems need systematic checking; a fluent answer may silently break constraints.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's customer-success manager wants a better onboarding email sequence for new business customers. She has the current five emails and open-rate data.
questions.question: How can Claude best support the redesign?

options.A: Share the current emails and data, ask for diagnosed weak points and two alternative sequences, then test with a small group.
options.B: Replace the whole sequence for new customers with Claude's first redesign, so results are measurable as quickly as possible.
options.C: Ask Claude to predict the open rate each new email will achieve, so she can pick the strongest sequence before sending anything.
options.D: Ask Claude to write a brand-new sequence without seeing the current one.

questions.explanation: Solution design with Claude works well as an iterative loop: give it the current state and evidence, ask for options with reasoning, and test before scaling.

why_incorrect.B: Rolling out an untested redesign to everyone removes the chance to learn and adjust.
why_incorrect.C: Claude cannot reliably predict precise future metrics; testing is needed.
why_incorrect.D: Without the current emails and data, Claude cannot build on what is working or fix what is not.

questions.scenario: Adatum Insurance's claims team has designed a new intake form with Claude's help. Before rollout, the team lead wants to find weaknesses in the design.
questions.question: Which use of Claude is most valuable at this stage?

options.A: Ask Claude to critique the design as a first-time claimant, a claims handler and an auditor, listing problems and fixes.
options.B: Ask Claude to add more fields to the form, so that every possible piece of information is captured at intake.
options.C: Ask Claude to confirm that the design meets good-practice standards, so the team has evidence of quality before rollout.
options.D: Ask Claude to add the company logo to every field.

questions.explanation: Claude is useful as a critical reviewer when asked to take specific stakeholder perspectives and identify concrete problems. Framing the request as critique rather than confirmation produces more useful feedback.

why_incorrect.B: Length is not the goal; a longer form may reduce completion rates.
why_incorrect.C: Seeking confirmation invites agreement rather than a critical review.
why_incorrect.D: Branding does not uncover design weaknesses.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's HR team used Claude to draft a new hybrid-working policy. The first draft was well received by managers but employees raised concerns in a pilot survey.
questions.question: Which TWO next steps represent good iteration?

options.A: Ignore the survey because managers approved the draft.
options.B: Give Claude the survey comments, ask it to group the concerns and suggest specific policy changes for each group.
options.C: Ask Claude to rewrite the survey comments in a more constructive, positive tone before sharing them with the policy group.
options.D: Produce a revised draft and a short change log explaining what changed and why, then re-test with a small employee group.
options.E: Start again from a blank page with a new prompt, so that the second draft is not anchored on the wording of the first.

questions.explanation: Iteration uses feedback as input: analyse it, make targeted changes, document what changed and validate again. This keeps what worked and fixes what did not.

why_incorrect.A: Employee feedback is evidence about whether the policy will work; ignoring it defeats the pilot.
why_incorrect.C: Altering feedback hides the problems the iteration is meant to fix.
why_incorrect.E: Discarding the draft throws away the parts managers already supported.

questions.scenario: Bellows College designed a Claude-assisted process in which advisers draft course-recommendation emails for students. After a month, advisers say they spend as long fixing drafts as they used to spend writing.
questions.question: What is the best first step in redesigning the process?

options.A: Sample drafts with advisers' edits, ask Claude to categorise the corrections, and fix the commonest causes.
options.B: Ask advisers to send drafts with fewer edits, since small imperfections matter less than the time saved.
options.C: Stop the process, since a month of extra editing shows that Claude is not suited to drafting advice for students.
options.D: Switch to the most capable model straight away, since drafting quality is mainly determined by model size.

questions.explanation: When a design underperforms, study the evidence. Categorising human corrections reveals whether the problem lies in missing context, unclear instructions or the wrong task split, and points to targeted fixes.

why_incorrect.B: Sending uncorrected drafts would expose students to errors.
why_incorrect.C: The evidence points to fixable causes; analysing the edits shows what to change.
why_incorrect.D: Changing the model without understanding the corrections may not address the real cause.

questions.scenario: Southridge Video's finance team spends hours each month writing commentary on budget variances. The numbers come from a spreadsheet; the commentary follows a standard structure and is reviewed by the finance manager.
questions.question: Which integration approach augments the workflow sensibly?

options.A: A Project with the template and style guidance; analysts upload the month's variance table and the manager reviews Claude's draft as before.
options.B: Ask Claude to estimate the variances instead of using the spreadsheet figures.
options.C: Keep the process fully manual because finance content is too sensitive for any assistance.
options.D: Let Claude write the commentary and publish it straight to the board pack, since the numbers come directly from the spreadsheet.

questions.explanation: Good integration augments existing steps: Claude takes on drafting from authoritative inputs, while existing controls such as manager review stay in place.

why_incorrect.B: Estimates would replace accurate source numbers with guesses.
why_incorrect.C: With appropriate review and data handling, drafting assistance is a common, sensible augmentation.
why_incorrect.D: Removing the existing review step increases risk for financial reporting.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending's operations team wants to redesign, not just speed up, how it handles internal policy questions from 600 staff. Today, questions arrive by email and two specialists answer them manually.
questions.question: Which TWO design elements are most important in the redesigned workflow?

options.A: A shared Project with curated, approved policy documents and instructions to cite the relevant section and refer people to specialists when unsure.
options.B: Instructing Claude to answer every question even when the policy is silent.
options.C: Removing the two specialists from the process once Claude is available, so their time can be moved to other work and costs fall.
options.D: An escalation path where unusual or high-impact questions go to the specialists, whose answers then improve the knowledge base.
options.E: Letting each staff member upload their own copies of the policies to personal chats, so they can ask questions in the way that suits them.

questions.explanation: Redesigning a workflow means rethinking roles: Claude handles routine questions from curated sources, specialists handle exceptions and maintain the knowledge, and a feedback loop keeps improving the system.

why_incorrect.B: Answering beyond the policy invites invented answers; escalation is safer.
why_incorrect.C: Specialists remain essential for edge cases, accountability and keeping the knowledge base accurate.
why_incorrect.E: Unmanaged copies diverge and lead to inconsistent answers.

questions.scenario: Proseware Education rolled out Claude for drafting parent newsletters. Adoption is low: teachers say it is "one more tool" and they forget to use it.
questions.question: Which change is most likely to improve adoption?

options.A: Send teachers a monthly reminder email that the tool is available, with a link to the login page.
options.B: Fit Claude into the existing routine, with a shared Project already set up with the template and examples and a short how-to guide.
options.C: Send teachers a detailed explainer on how language models work, so they understand the tool well enough to use it.
options.D: Require newsletters to be drafted entirely by Claude from now on, so that using it becomes the default habit.

questions.explanation: Adoption improves when Claude fits naturally into existing routines, with pre-configured Projects and clear guidance at the point of work, rather than being an extra, separate step.

why_incorrect.A: Reminders do not remove the barrier; the tool still sits outside the teachers' routine.
why_incorrect.C: Background knowledge helps, but the barrier is workflow fit rather than theory.
why_incorrect.D: Mandating full automation ignores teachers' judgement and may reduce quality and trust.

questions.scenario: A team manager at Humongous Insurance asks about the difference between using Claude to augment a workflow and using it to redesign one.
questions.question: Which statement best captures the difference?

options.A: Redesigning means removing human involvement from the process, while augmenting keeps people doing every step.
options.B: There is no difference; both mean adding Claude to a process.
options.C: Augmenting means using a smaller, cheaper model; redesigning means moving the work to the most capable model available.
options.D: Augmenting improves existing steps; redesigning rethinks the steps and roles around what Claude and people do best.

questions.explanation: Augmentation keeps the workflow shape and improves individual steps. Redesign reconsiders which steps exist and who does them, which can unlock larger gains but needs more change management.

why_incorrect.A: Redesign changes roles; human oversight usually remains, especially for important decisions.
why_incorrect.B: They differ in scope: one keeps the process shape, the other changes it.
why_incorrect.C: Model size is unrelated to whether a workflow is augmented or redesigned.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's marketing director asks Aisha whether Claude can "write all our social posts from now on, with no one checking them."
questions.question: Which response communicates value and limitations most accurately?

options.A: Claude can draft posts quickly in the brand voice, but a person should check accuracy, tone and timing before publishing.
options.B: No, Claude is not suitable for marketing content, because social posts need a human creative touch that AI cannot provide.
options.C: Yes, Claude is reliable for marketing content, so once the brand voice is set up the posts can be published as they are.
options.D: Yes, provided the posts stay short, because short posts leave very little room for errors to appear.

questions.explanation: Credible communication about Claude is balanced: state concrete benefits and the specific limitations, along with the controls that manage them.

why_incorrect.B: Understating value ignores clear time savings in drafting.
why_incorrect.C: Overstating reliability sets unrealistic expectations and risks public errors.
why_incorrect.D: Short posts can still contain errors or poor timing; length does not remove the need for review.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health's operations manager is preparing a one-page summary for executives after a three-month Claude pilot in the scheduling team.
questions.question: Which TWO items make the summary most credible?

options.A: Projected savings from extending Claude to every department, extrapolated from the scheduling team's results, to show the full opportunity.
options.B: Selected positive quotes with negative feedback removed.
options.C: Measured results against the baseline, such as average time to draft a schedule notice before and after the pilot.
options.D: Known limitations seen in the pilot and the controls the team uses to manage them.
options.E: A statement that the model is the most advanced available, as proof of value.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders trust evidence: measured outcomes against a baseline, plus an honest account of limitations and how they are handled.

why_incorrect.A: Untested extrapolation weakens credibility; executives need evidence.
why_incorrect.B: Omitting negative feedback misrepresents the pilot and undermines trust.
why_incorrect.E: Model reputation does not demonstrate value for this team's work.

questions.scenario: A frontline team at Acme Logistics fears that Claude will be used to monitor them and replace their jobs. Their manager needs to introduce a Claude pilot for drafting delivery-exception notices.
questions.question: Which communication approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Tell the team that AI will make their roles obsolete, so they should adapt quickly.
options.B: Promise the team that nothing about their work or roles will change as a result of the pilot, to reduce anxiety.
options.C: Explain the specific task, what stays with the team (judgement and approval), how data is handled, and invite feedback.
options.D: Say nothing about the pilot until it is complete, so the team is not distracted and the results are not influenced.

questions.explanation: Transparent, specific communication builds trust: be clear about scope, human responsibilities, data handling and how feedback will be used, without overpromising in either direction.

why_incorrect.A: This is speculative, increases anxiety and misrepresents a narrow drafting pilot.
why_incorrect.B: An absolute promise is unlikely to be accurate and can damage trust later.
why_incorrect.D: Secrecy increases mistrust and denies the team a chance to shape the pilot.

questions.scenario: After a successful pilot, Datum Corp's CFO asks for Claude to be rolled out to the legal team with the claim that it will "eliminate contract errors." The pilot was in marketing.
questions.question: How should the programme lead respond?

options.A: Decline any legal use, because legal work is too complex for AI and the marketing pilot proves nothing about it.
options.B: Agree to the claim but quietly add reviewers later.
options.C: Agree, since the legal team would use the same tool and similar prompts as marketing.
options.D: Explain that marketing results do not transfer directly, propose a scoped legal pilot with success measures and review, and drop the error claim.

questions.explanation: Managing expectations means correcting overstatements, separating evidence from extrapolation, and proposing a measured way to test value in the new context.

why_incorrect.A: A carefully scoped and reviewed pilot can test value; a blanket refusal is unnecessary.
why_incorrect.B: Accepting an inaccurate claim misleads stakeholders even if controls are added afterwards.
why_incorrect.C: Different tasks and risk levels mean results must be validated per use case, whatever the tool.

questions.scenario: Carmen is setting up a Project at Wingtip Events for writing post-event reports. Every report must use the same section order, a neutral tone and the company's attendance-metric definitions.
questions.question: Where should each piece of information go?

options.A: Put the whole brief in the first message of each new chat, so that each report starts with a complete and current brief.
options.B: Section order and tone in the Project instructions; the metric definitions document in Project knowledge.
options.C: Put the metric definitions in Claude's account-level memory.
options.D: Upload the tone and section guidance as a knowledge file and leave the Project instructions empty, to keep things in one place.

questions.explanation: Project instructions shape how Claude behaves in every chat in the Project (role, tone, format). Project knowledge holds reference material Claude should draw on. Using each for its purpose keeps the Project predictable.

why_incorrect.A: Repeating set-up in every chat is error-prone; Projects exist to hold this persistently.
why_incorrect.C: Reference material that must be applied exactly belongs in Project knowledge, not in memory that captures selected topics.
why_incorrect.D: Behavioural guidance such as tone and structure belongs in instructions, which tell Claude how to respond in every chat.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel is creating a shared Project for its 12-person itinerary team on a Team plan. A senior planner will maintain it.
questions.question: Which TWO configuration choices are sound?

options.A: Upload every itinerary from the past ten years, so Claude has the widest possible set of examples to draw on for new trips.
options.B: Leave the instructions blank so each planner can phrase their own each time.
options.C: Give the senior planner "Can edit" access and most members "Can view" access, so they can chat but not change the set-up.
options.D: Give every team member edit access, so that anyone who finds a useful supplier document can add it to the knowledge straight away.
options.E: Upload only current, approved supplier guides and itinerary templates to the Project knowledge.

questions.explanation: On Team and Enterprise plans, Projects can be shared with view or edit permissions. Restricting edit rights to an owner and curating knowledge to current, relevant material keeps a shared Project reliable.

why_incorrect.A: Bulk uploads of loosely relevant material add noise and make answers less focused.
why_incorrect.B: Shared instructions are what make outputs consistent across the team.
why_incorrect.D: Uncontrolled edits lead to conflicting or outdated knowledge and inconsistent answers.

questions.scenario: Jamal at Trey Research uploaded a 400-page set of research reports to a Project on a paid plan. Claude still answers questions using the material but now seems to draw on a few relevant passages rather than the whole set at once.
questions.question: What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Knowledge near the context limit made the Project switch to retrieval, which finds the relevant passages.
options.B: The upload partly failed, so Claude sees just some of the reports and is filling the gaps from general knowledge.
options.C: Projects read the opening pages of each file, so long reports need to be split into many smaller uploads.
options.D: Claude ignores Project knowledge whenever memory is turned on.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, on paid plans, when Project knowledge approaches the context limit Claude automatically uses retrieval to find relevant parts of the knowledge, which expands capacity. Clear, well-structured documents help retrieval find the right passages.

why_incorrect.B: Claude is answering accurately from the reports, which points to retrieval selecting passages rather than a failed upload.
why_incorrect.C: There is no rule that Projects read the opening pages of files; large knowledge bases are handled through retrieval on paid plans.
why_incorrect.D: Memory and Project knowledge are separate features; memory does not disable knowledge.

questions.scenario: Bellows College's admissions office plans one Project for both undergraduate and postgraduate enquiries. The two have different deadlines, fees and tone requirements, and staff keep getting answers that mix them up.
questions.question: What is the best configuration change?

options.A: Create separate Projects for undergraduate and postgraduate enquiries, each with its own instructions and knowledge.
options.B: Use a standalone chat without a Project for every enquiry.
options.C: Keep one Project and add an instruction to "be careful to use the correct programme's information" in every answer.
options.D: Keep one Project and remove the fee documents so that Claude cannot quote the wrong fees.

questions.explanation: Projects work best when scoped to a coherent body of work. When two audiences need different rules and facts, separate Projects prevent cross-contamination and make each easier to maintain.

why_incorrect.B: This loses the persistent instructions and knowledge entirely.
why_incorrect.C: A vague instruction does not stop Claude drawing on the wrong set of fees and deadlines.
why_incorrect.D: Removing needed information makes the Project less useful rather than more accurate.

questions.scenario: Isabel at Fabrikam Retail uses the Gmail connector and asks Claude to summarise the PDF invoices attached to supplier emails from last week. Claude lists the emails and attachment names but cannot summarise the invoice contents.
questions.question: What is the most likely reason?

options.A: Claude cannot read any PDF in any context.
options.B: Gmail exposes message content and attachment metadata, not attachment contents; she should add the PDFs to the chat directly.
options.C: The Gmail connector has lost its authorisation, so it can see email headers but not files; she should disconnect and reconnect it.
options.D: Invoice PDFs need a more capable model to interpret tables, so she should switch models and ask again.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, the Gmail connector exposes message content and attachment metadata, not attachment contents. Knowing each connector's scope helps users pick the right route for the data they need.

why_incorrect.A: Claude can read PDFs uploaded directly or retrieved from supported sources such as Drive.
why_incorrect.C: Listing emails and attachment names shows it is working within its normal scope.
why_incorrect.D: Model choice does not change what data the connector makes available.

questions.scenario: Tom at Alpine Ski House wants a private Project to always use the latest version of the team's pricing guide, which colleagues edit in Google Docs.
questions.question: What is the best approach?

options.A: Ask colleagues to email him changes so he can tell Claude about them.
options.B: Add the Google Doc from Google Drive, so Claude uses the latest synced version.
options.C: Copy the full text of the guide into the Project instructions, so Claude reads it first in each chat.
options.D: Download a PDF of the guide on the first of each month and upload it to the Project, deleting the previous copy each time.

questions.explanation: Google Docs added to chats and Projects through the Drive connector sync from Drive, so Claude uses the latest version. As of 2026-10-24, adding Drive files to Project knowledge is available for private Projects.

why_incorrect.A: This is slow, error-prone and depends on people remembering to send updates.
why_incorrect.C: Instructions are for guidance on behaviour; pasted reference text goes stale and bloats the instructions.
why_incorrect.D: Manual re-uploads can be forgotten and create stale copies, while a Drive-linked Doc stays current.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending, on an Enterprise plan, is enabling the Google Drive connector for the first time.
questions.question: Which TWO statements about access and administration are accurate?

options.A: An organisation Owner must enable the connector before members can connect their own Google accounts.
options.B: Once one administrator connects their Google account, every member can search every file in the company Drive through Claude.
options.C: The connector respects each user's existing Google permissions, so Claude can only reach files that user can access.
options.D: Content from connected Drive files is automatically copied into the shared knowledge of every Project in the organisation.
options.E: Users can bypass the Owner setting by installing the connector in a personal browser.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, on Team and Enterprise plans an Owner enables Google Workspace connectors first; then each member authenticates with their own account, and Claude's access mirrors that user's Google permissions.

why_incorrect.B: Each user authenticates individually and access mirrors their own Google permissions.
why_incorrect.D: Connector content is pulled into the chats and Projects where it is used; it is not automatically copied into every Project.
why_incorrect.E: Organisation controls govern connector availability for members on Team and Enterprise plans.

questions.scenario: Claude summarised a Google Slides deck from Drive for Wei at Southridge Video, but missed all the numbers shown in the embedded chart images.
questions.question: What explains this, and what should Wei do?

options.A: The deck is too long; split it into one-slide files.
options.B: The Drive connector extracts text only, so embedded images are skipped; provide the figures as text or upload the charts.
options.C: Slides files are read in part through the Drive connector, so Wei should export the deck to Word first.
options.D: Claude declines to report numbers from presentations, to avoid misquoting financial data, so the figures must be typed in.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, the Drive connector reads text from supported files and does not process images embedded in documents. Knowing this helps users spot gaps and supply missing visual data another way.

why_incorrect.A: Length is not the cause; images would still be skipped in shorter files.
why_incorrect.C: Slides text is read; only the embedded images are skipped.
why_incorrect.D: There is no such refusal; the issue is how content is extracted from Drive files.

questions.scenario: Rosa is writing Project instructions for Coho Winery's sales team. Her draft says: "Be helpful and professional."
questions.question: Which revision makes the instructions most effective?

options.A: State the users, supported tasks, tone and format, which knowledge files to rely on, and what to do when information is missing.
options.B: Add "IMPORTANT: be helpful and accurate" in capitals at the top so Claude takes it seriously.
options.C: Replace it with a detailed list of words, phrases and topics Claude must avoid with customers.
options.D: Keep it short and let Claude infer the rest from the knowledge files, since they describe the service.

questions.explanation: Strong system-level instructions explain the context and the expected behaviour: audience, purpose, style, sources and how to handle uncertainty. Specific guidance produces consistent results across chats.

why_incorrect.B: Emphasis does not add the missing context about users, tasks or format.
why_incorrect.C: A banned-word list ignores the core guidance on role, tasks and format.
why_incorrect.D: Knowledge files describe the service, not the users, tone, format or what to do when information is missing; outputs will vary.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Clinics' HR team is writing instructions for a Project that answers staff questions about leave policies using uploaded policy documents.
questions.question: Which THREE instructions are most appropriate?

options.A: Use plain language and keep answers under 150 words unless the person asks for more detail.
options.B: If the documents are unclear, choose the interpretation most favourable to the employee.
options.C: Avoid mentioning that answers come from documents, so they sound more authoritative.
options.D: If the documents do not cover a question, say so and direct the person to the HR inbox.
options.E: Answer only from the uploaded policy documents and name the policy and section used.

questions.explanation: Effective instructions define the source of truth, the behaviour when the source is silent, and the expected format. Escalating uncertain cases and citing sources keeps answers verifiable.

why_incorrect.B: Resolving ambiguity on Claude's own judgement can produce inconsistent, unauthorised answers; unclear cases should be escalated.
why_incorrect.C: Hiding sources makes answers harder to verify and undermines trust.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's Project instructions contain both "Always respond in bullet points" and, later, "Write responses as flowing paragraphs suitable for emails." Outputs alternate unpredictably between the two.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Delete the instructions entirely and specify format in each chat.
options.B: Add a further instruction telling Claude to choose whichever format best suits each request, so it can resolve the conflict itself.
options.C: Move the bullet-point rule to the top of the instructions, because the earliest instruction is the one Claude gives priority.
options.D: State when each format applies, for example bullets for internal notes and paragraphs for customer emails.

questions.explanation: Contradictory instructions produce inconsistent results. Review instructions for conflicts and make conditions explicit so Claude knows which rule applies in which situation.

why_incorrect.A: This removes useful shared guidance instead of fixing the conflict.
why_incorrect.B: This leaves the conflict unresolved and the outputs still unpredictable.
why_incorrect.C: Reordering does not clarify intent; both rules still apply to the same situations.

questions.scenario: A manager at Humongous Insurance asks why her Project instructions explain the reasons behind rules, such as "Avoid jargon because most readers are new policyholders", instead of just listing the rules.
questions.question: What is the main benefit of giving reasons?

options.A: Reasons make instructions longer and more detailed, and longer instructions consistently produce better results.
options.B: Claude tends to ignore rules that have no reason attached, so every rule needs a justification to be followed.
options.C: Reasons mainly help auditors and colleagues understand the instructions later, rather than affecting answers.
options.D: Knowing why a rule exists helps Claude apply it sensibly in situations the rule did not anticipate.

questions.explanation: Explaining the purpose behind an instruction lets Claude generalise it correctly, for example simplifying technical terms in a new kind of document because it understands who the readers are.

why_incorrect.A: Length alone does not improve results; the value comes from the context reasons provide.
why_incorrect.B: Claude follows clear rules without reasons; reasons improve judgement in edge cases.
why_incorrect.C: Reasons do help people, but the main benefit is that Claude applies the rule better in unanticipated cases.

questions.scenario: Acme Logistics' shared customs-guidance Project has grown over a year. Several team members have uploaded slightly different versions of the same export checklist, and answers sometimes quote different requirements.
questions.question: What should the Project owner do?

options.A: Add an instruction telling Claude to combine the requirements from every version, so no requirement is missed.
options.B: Leave the versions in the knowledge, so Claude can compare them and choose the most complete one for each answer.
options.C: Keep one approved, dated version of the checklist, remove the duplicates, and agree who may update it.
options.D: Delete the Project and start a new one each quarter.

questions.explanation: Knowledge needs curation. One approved, dated version per document, plus clear ownership of changes, keeps answers consistent.

why_incorrect.A: Combining conflicting versions can produce requirements the approved checklist does not contain; the fix is one approved version.
why_incorrect.B: Conflicting versions in knowledge cause conflicting answers; Claude cannot know which is approved.
why_incorrect.D: Rebuilding regularly loses useful configuration and does not fix the version-control problem.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's operations team relies on six shared Projects. The team lead wants a lightweight maintenance routine.
questions.question: Which TWO practices should the routine include?

options.A: A small set of standard test questions run after each significant change to confirm answers are still correct.
options.B: A named owner for each Project who reviews instructions and knowledge on a regular schedule, such as quarterly.
options.C: Add every new document the team receives to every Project automatically, so that the knowledge in each Project stays complete.
options.D: Review a Project when users report a serious error, rather than on a fixed schedule.
options.E: Allow anyone on the team to edit instructions at any time without notice, so improvements reach everyone as quickly as possible.

questions.explanation: Ownership, scheduled reviews and simple regression checks with known questions are effective ways to keep configurations reliable as content and needs change.

why_incorrect.C: Indiscriminate additions dilute knowledge and introduce conflicts.
why_incorrect.D: Purely reactive maintenance lets errors reach people before they are caught.
why_incorrect.E: Unmanaged edits make behaviour change unexpectedly and are hard to trace.

questions.scenario: Graphic Design Institute's student-services team changed its Project instructions to make answers shorter. Afterwards, answers are shorter but no longer include the link to the booking system, which used to appear every time.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause, and the best fix?

options.A: The Project knowledge was automatically deleted.
options.B: Shorter answers cannot contain links, so the team must choose between brevity and including the booking link.
options.C: The booking system may be offline, and Claude stops mentioning links to systems that are unavailable.
options.D: The edit weakened the booking-link instruction; restore it explicitly and re-run standard test questions after each change.

questions.explanation: Changes to instructions can have unintended side effects. Compare the old and new versions, restore the lost requirement and test with a standard question set after every edit.

why_incorrect.A: Knowledge does not disappear because of an instruction edit; the instructions changed.
why_incorrect.B: Short answers can include links if instructed.
why_incorrect.C: Claude is not checking the system's status; the change coincides with the instruction edit.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's sales team installed a custom Skill from an external website six months ago. A new version is now available from the same site, and the team wants to install it immediately.
questions.question: What is the most responsible maintenance step?

options.A: Disable code execution permanently to avoid any Skill risk.
options.B: Install it straight away, because the earlier version from the same site has worked safely for six months.
options.C: Review the new version's files, instructions and external connections before enabling it.
options.D: Enable it for the whole organisation first, then ask users to report anything unusual over the following week.

questions.explanation: Skills can include instructions and code that influence Claude's actions. Treat updates from less-trusted sources like new software: review the contents, check for unexpected network access, and only then enable them.

why_incorrect.A: Skills rely on code execution; a blanket disable removes their benefit instead of managing the risk.
why_incorrect.B: A previous version being safe does not guarantee the new one is; each version should be reviewed.
why_incorrect.D: Broad rollout before review spreads any risk across all users.

questions.scenario: Adatum Insurance's team is listing possible Claude uses: drafting internal training quizzes, summarising public industry reports, brainstorming event themes, and automatically deciding which claims are denied with no human involvement.
questions.question: Which proposed use is most clearly inappropriate as described?

options.A: Drafting internal training quizzes on claims procedures for new staff.
options.B: Brainstorming themes and session titles for the annual customer event.
options.C: Summarising public industry reports on claims trends for the leadership team.
options.D: Automatically deciding claim denials with no human involvement.

questions.explanation: Decisions with significant consequences for individuals, such as insurance claim denials, should not be fully automated without human oversight. Anthropic's Usage Policy sets additional requirements for high-risk uses that affect people's access to services, including human review.

why_incorrect.A: This is a low-risk drafting task where a human can easily check the result.
why_incorrect.B: Brainstorming is low-stakes and benefits from Claude's creativity.
why_incorrect.C: Summarising public material is a standard, low-risk use, with normal accuracy checks.

questions.scenario: Proseware Education's teachers are discussing ways to use Claude with students' work.
questions.question: Which TWO uses are appropriate, assuming school policy allows them?

options.A: Writing essays for students to submit as their own work.
options.B: Asking Claude to determine whether a student is lying about being ill.
options.C: Drafting general feedback themes on a set of anonymised essays, which the teacher then reviews and personalises.
options.D: Generating varied practice questions on a topic for revision.
options.E: Assigning final grades automatically to save teacher time, with teachers reading just the essays Claude marks as borderline.

questions.explanation: Appropriate uses support people's judgement and are easy to check, such as practice material and draft feedback. Inappropriate uses hand consequential judgements to Claude or enable dishonesty.

why_incorrect.A: This undermines academic integrity and the purpose of assessment.
why_incorrect.B: Claude cannot reliably make such a judgement, and using it this way could unfairly harm the student.
why_incorrect.E: Final grading has real consequences for students and needs the teacher's judgement.

questions.scenario: A recruiter at Datum Corp wants to paste 200 CVs into Claude and ask it to "reject anyone who doesn't seem like a culture fit."
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.A: Ask Claude to infer candidates' ages from graduation years to help screening.
options.B: Proceed, but start with the first 50 CVs and review a few rejections to see whether the results look sensible.
options.C: Proceed as asked, because Claude applies the same standard to every CV and is therefore free from the biases people have.
options.D: Reframe it: summarise CVs against defined, job-related criteria, with a recruiter making and recording decisions.

questions.explanation: Employment decisions are high-impact. Use clear, job-related criteria, keep humans accountable for decisions, and avoid vague criteria or inferences about protected characteristics.

why_incorrect.A: Inferring protected characteristics for screening creates discrimination risk.
why_incorrect.B: Reducing the number does not address the inappropriate criterion or lack of human decision-making.
why_incorrect.C: Models can reflect biases, and "culture fit" is a vague criterion that can mask discrimination.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's social media lead asks Claude to write 50 five-star customer reviews to post on review sites under made-up names for a new store.
questions.question: Why is this inappropriate, and what is a better alternative?

options.A: It is acceptable as long as the reviews are well written and describe things the store genuinely offers.
options.B: It is acceptable if each review is written in a different style, so the reviews read as natural and varied.
options.C: It is fine if staff post the reviews from their own personal accounts instead of under made-up names.
options.D: Fake reviews deceive consumers and breach usage policies; instead, invite genuine customers to leave honest reviews.

questions.explanation: Using Claude to create deceptive content, such as fake reviews presented as genuine, is inappropriate. Claude can instead support honest approaches that achieve the same business goal.

why_incorrect.A: Even accurate descriptions are deceptive when presented as reviews from customers who do not exist.
why_incorrect.B: Variety makes the deception harder to spot, not acceptable.
why_incorrect.C: Reviews written by staff and presented as customer opinions are still deceptive, whoever posts them.

questions.scenario: A new employee at Coho Winery asks how to tell whether a task is a good fit for Claude.
questions.question: Which rule of thumb is most useful?

options.A: Tasks are a good fit when Claude can complete them without any human involvement.
options.B: Tasks involving numbers or data are the best fit, since writing tasks depend too much on personal judgement.
options.C: Tasks where the output can be checked and errors are manageable, or where a human makes the final call.
options.D: Any task is a good fit as long as it saves a meaningful amount of time compared with doing it by hand.

questions.explanation: Assess fit by verifiability, consequence of errors and the presence of human decision-making, not only by convenience.

why_incorrect.A: Many of the best uses combine Claude's drafting with human judgement.
why_incorrect.B: Writing is one of Claude's main strengths.
why_incorrect.D: Time saved does not justify uses that are high-risk, deceptive or impossible to verify.

questions.scenario: Lena, a team manager at Lucerne Clinics, wants Claude to help rewrite a sick-leave summary that contains staff names and medical diagnoses. Her organisation has an approved Claude Enterprise workspace and a policy on health data.
questions.question: What should she do first?

options.A: Check the policy on health data; if allowed, use only the approved workspace, otherwise remove identifying details first.
options.B: Paste it anywhere, because Claude does not store anything.
options.C: Ask Claude whether it is permitted to process health data, and follow its answer, since it knows its own data handling.
options.D: Paste it into her personal free account, which is quicker, and delete the chat afterwards so nothing is kept.

questions.explanation: Health information is highly sensitive. Follow organisational policy, use the approved environment, and minimise or de-identify data where possible.

why_incorrect.B: Data handling depends on the account, settings and policies; it is not safe to assume nothing is retained.
why_incorrect.C: Claude cannot know her organisation's policies; the policy owner decides.
why_incorrect.D: Personal accounts may not have the organisation's contractual and administrative protections for sensitive data.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending's marketing team wants to use Claude to analyse customer feedback that includes names, email addresses and free-text comments.
questions.question: Which TWO practices best reduce privacy risk while keeping the analysis useful?

options.A: Use the organisation's approved Claude workspace that is covered by its data agreements.
options.B: Remove names and email addresses before analysis, since themes do not depend on identity.
options.C: Ask Claude to look up each customer's social media profiles to enrich the analysis.
options.D: Keep the identifiers in the data, so Claude can link related comments from the same customer and personalise each finding.
options.E: Share the analysis chat publicly so other teams can learn from it.

questions.explanation: Data minimisation and approved environments are core privacy practices: share only what the task needs, and use tools covered by the organisation's agreements and controls.

why_incorrect.C: Compiling extra personal data goes beyond the purpose and increases privacy risk.
why_incorrect.D: Identifiers add risk without improving theme analysis.
why_incorrect.E: Publicly sharing a chat containing customer data could expose personal information.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's strategy team is evaluating a confidential acquisition. An analyst wants to use the research feature with connectors to Drive and Gmail to gather everything related to the target company.
questions.question: What is the most important consideration?

options.A: Use a personal account for the research, which keeps the confidential deal details away from the bank's shared systems.
options.B: Confirm policy allows it, use the approved workspace, and connect only the needed sources, since research reads whatever they can access.
options.C: Paste the deal details into a public forum to get more opinions.
options.D: Connect every available connector, so the research is as complete as possible and nothing relevant to the target is missed.

questions.explanation: Connectors give Claude access to data in connected accounts. Limit connections to what is needed and keep confidential work in approved, governed environments.

why_incorrect.A: Avoiding organisational oversight for confidential work is a policy and security violation.
why_incorrect.C: Public disclosure of confidential deal information is a serious breach.
why_incorrect.D: Broad connector access exposes more confidential data than the task needs.

questions.scenario: A Graphic Design Institute administrator in the EU wants Claude to draft letters to students using enrolment data. Their data protection officer asks about lawful processing.
questions.question: Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Proceed once Claude confirms that the processing is lawful under the relevant data protection rules.
options.B: Proceed, because drafting letters is a routine administrative task and does not count as processing personal data.
options.C: Send the full enrolment database, so the letters can be as personalised and accurate as possible.
options.D: Work with the data protection officer on purpose, legal basis and minimum data, then use only an approved account.

questions.explanation: Regulatory requirements apply to AI-assisted processing like any other. Involve accountable roles, confirm purpose and legal basis, minimise data and use approved tools.

why_incorrect.A: Legal determinations belong to the organisation's accountable roles, not to Claude.
why_incorrect.B: Using enrolment data to draft letters is processing personal data, and data protection obligations apply whatever tool is used.
why_incorrect.C: Sending more data than needed conflicts with data minimisation.

questions.scenario: Tom at Acme Logistics asks whether there is anything he should never paste into Claude, even in the approved company workspace.
questions.question: Which answer best reflects good practice?

options.A: Never paste secrets such as passwords, keys or tokens, and follow policy for other restricted data.
options.B: Anything already circulated by email inside the company is safe to paste, since it has already left the original system.
options.C: In the approved workspace, system passwords and other restricted data are fine to include, because company agreements cover it.
options.D: Personal data is the main concern; internal technical material such as configuration files can be pasted once names are removed.

questions.explanation: Some information, such as credentials, should never be entered into a chat. Other categories depend on policy, environment and need.

why_incorrect.B: Internal circulation does not change how sensitive information is; secrets in an email are still secrets.
why_incorrect.C: Credentials should not be shared in chat in any workspace; their exposure can lead to account compromise.
why_incorrect.D: Configuration files often contain passwords, keys or tokens, which should not be pasted; other internal data depends on policy.

questions.scenario: Southridge Video's AI policy requires staff to use the company's Claude Team workspace for work and to label AI-assisted public content. Ben prefers his personal account because he has his own Projects set up there.
questions.question: What should Ben do?

options.A: Ask a colleague to approve an exception informally over chat.
options.B: Use his personal account for the most confidential work, where keeping things separate from shared systems matters most.
options.C: Keep using his personal account for work, since his Projects are already set up there and the outputs are the same.
options.D: Recreate the Projects in the company workspace without copying restricted data, and follow the labelling rule.

questions.explanation: Organisational AI policies define approved tools and practices. Follow them, and use formal exception routes when there is a genuine need.

why_incorrect.A: Exceptions should go through the policy's formal process, not informal approval.
why_incorrect.B: Confidential work is exactly what should stay in the governed workspace.
why_incorrect.C: Convenience does not override policy; personal accounts sit outside company controls.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail is writing its first AI usage policy for Claude across business teams.
questions.question: Which THREE elements should the policy include?

options.A: Which tools and plans are approved for work use.
options.B: A rule that the most capable available model is used for every task, so quality does not depend on individual choices.
options.C: Human review requirements for AI-assisted output, by risk level.
options.D: A requirement that staff do not mention AI use to customers, to protect the company's brand.
options.E: Data classifications that may or may not be used with Claude, with examples.

questions.explanation: Effective AI policies cover approved tools, data handling rules and review requirements scaled to risk, along with clear ownership and an exception process.

why_incorrect.B: Model choice is a task-level decision, not a governance requirement.
why_incorrect.D: Concealment conflicts with transparency expectations and some disclosure obligations.

questions.scenario: An audit at Humongous Insurance finds that several teams uploaded customer complaint files to Projects shared with the whole organisation, although policy restricts them to the complaints team.
questions.question: What is the best corrective action?

options.A: Ask Claude in each Project to forget the complaint files so they are no longer used.
options.B: Delete every Project across the organisation and start again with stricter rules.
options.C: Limit sharing to the complaints team, remove files where not allowed, report it, and reinforce training.
options.D: Take no action, since the files stayed with employees and nothing left the organisation.

questions.explanation: Governance failures need containment (fix access), correction (remove data where it does not belong), reporting and prevention (training and configuration).

why_incorrect.A: Access is controlled by sharing settings and file management, not by asking Claude.
why_incorrect.B: This is disproportionate and destroys legitimate work.
why_incorrect.D: Internal over-sharing still breaches the policy and can expose customers' data.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel's IT owner is deciding whether members on the company's Enterprise plan may let Claude send emails through the Gmail connector without approving each message.
questions.question: Which approach best aligns with good governance?

options.A: Let each user decide without any guidance.
options.B: Disable every connector permanently, since any connector that can act on email is too risky to allow.
options.C: Keep per-action approval for sending as the default, relaxing it only for reviewed, low-risk uses.
options.D: Allow automatic sending by default, since the Enterprise plan already provides strong security and it saves time.

questions.explanation: As of 2026-10-24, Owners can control whether members may run send, share, move and trash actions without per-action approval. Keeping human confirmation for actions with external effects is a sensible default.

why_incorrect.A: Unguided individual choices produce inconsistent risk across the organisation.
why_incorrect.B: This forgoes legitimate read-only benefits; governance can manage the risk proportionately.
why_incorrect.D: Removing approval for outbound communication increases the risk of mistaken or manipulated messages.

questions.scenario: A manager at Contoso Health asks who is responsible when a report drafted with Claude contains an error that reaches a client.
questions.question: Which statement reflects sound governance?

options.A: The people who used and approved the output remain accountable, which is why review matters.
options.B: The client is responsible, because recipients are expected to check anything they rely on.
options.C: Anthropic is responsible for errors in Claude's outputs, since the model generated the content.
options.D: Nobody can be held responsible, because errors from AI tools are unpredictable by nature.

questions.explanation: AI assistance does not transfer accountability. Governance assigns ownership for outputs and requires proportionate review before they are used.

why_incorrect.B: The sender is accountable for what they send.
why_incorrect.C: Organisations remain responsible for how they use and approve outputs.
why_incorrect.D: Unpredictability is a reason for review, not a removal of accountability.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Events used Claude to draft a keynote speech for its CEO. A journalist later asks whether AI was used.
questions.question: Which response is most ethical?

options.A: Explain that the speech was written entirely by AI, so the CEO should not be held responsible for any of its content.
options.B: Answer honestly that AI helped draft the speech and the CEO reviewed and owns it, in line with policy.
options.C: Say that the CEO wrote the speech personally, since the CEO approved the final text and AI help is an internal detail.
options.D: Refuse to comment and delete the drafts.

questions.explanation: Transparency about AI assistance, alongside clear human ownership of the content, supports trust.

why_incorrect.A: This is inaccurate and disowns responsibility for the content.
why_incorrect.C: Lying about AI use is deceptive and risks reputational harm if discovered.
why_incorrect.D: Destroying records to avoid scrutiny is not transparent.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Travel's marketing team wants to use Claude to produce persuasive campaign copy.
questions.question: Which TWO practices reflect ethical use?

options.A: Write copy that imitates a competitor's brand so customers confuse the two.
options.B: Use Claude to generate fake scarcity messages, such as "only 2 seats left" when that is untrue.
options.C: Make sure claims are truthful and substantiated, and avoid exploiting customers' fears or vulnerabilities.
options.D: Remove the small-print disclaimers from offers, so that the main message is clearer and the ads look more appealing.
options.E: Review copy for stereotypes or exclusionary language before publishing.

questions.explanation: Persuasion is legitimate when it is honest and respectful. Ethical use means truthful claims, no manipulation and inclusive language.

why_incorrect.A: Deliberately confusing customers is deceptive and may infringe rights.
why_incorrect.B: Fabricated scarcity is deceptive and manipulates customers.
why_incorrect.D: Removing required disclaimers misleads customers.

questions.scenario: Litware Publishing's editor wants to use Claude to write a book chapter "in the exact style" of a living novelist and publish it under the editor's name as original work.
questions.question: What is the main ethical concern, and the better path?

options.A: There is no concern, because a writing style cannot be owned and Claude produces new sentences rather than copying text.
options.B: Close imitation of a living author passed off as original raises authorship and IP concerns; develop an original voice instead.
options.C: Imitation is acceptable as long as no sentence is copied word for word from the author's books.
options.D: The concern is cost, because long chapters use more of the usage allowance.

questions.explanation: Using AI to imitate a specific living creator and present the result as original work raises ethical and legal questions. Original creation and honest attribution avoid them.

why_incorrect.A: Close imitation presented as original still raises authorship and possible infringement issues.
why_incorrect.C: Avoiding verbatim copying does not resolve passing off a close imitation of a living author as original work.
why_incorrect.D: Usage is not the ethical issue.

questions.scenario: Datum Corp's analyst asks Claude, with the web browsing and research tools on, to summarise a supplier's public web page. The page contains hidden text instructing AI assistants to say the supplier has perfect safety records.
questions.question: What does this illustrate, and how should the analyst respond?

options.A: Nothing to act on, because Claude reliably detects and ignores hidden instructions in web pages it reads.
options.B: A harmless formatting issue on the supplier's site, so the summary can be used once the odd text is ignored.
options.C: A sign the research tool is faulty; switch it off and paste the supplier's page text into the chat instead.
options.D: Indirect prompt injection; treat external content as untrusted, check the summary against other sources, and report it.

questions.explanation: Content retrieved from the web or connected sources can contain instructions intended to manipulate AI output. Treat it as untrusted, verify important claims and report attempts.

why_incorrect.A: Defences reduce risk but are not perfect; human verification still matters.
why_incorrect.B: Hidden instructions aimed at AI are a manipulation attempt, not a formatting issue.
why_incorrect.C: The problem is the page content, not the tool; pasted text can carry the same instructions and still needs treating as untrusted.

questions.scenario: Bellows College's ethics committee asks why over-reliance on AI tools is an ethical issue and not only a quality issue.
questions.question: Which answer is most accurate?

options.A: Over-reliance stops being a real risk once staff are trained to write good prompts.
options.B: Over-reliance matters mainly for technical staff, who might lose coding skills if they rely on AI assistants.
options.C: It can erode human skills and judgement, hide errors that affect people, and blur accountability.
options.D: Over-reliance is mainly a cost issue, because heavy use of AI tools increases subscription and usage spending.

questions.explanation: Responsible use keeps humans engaged and accountable. Over-reliance can let errors affect people unnoticed and weaken the human judgement that oversight depends on.

why_incorrect.A: Good prompts improve output but do not make it correct; reviewing and owning the result still matters.
why_incorrect.B: Any role that depends on AI output can be affected.
why_incorrect.D: The concern is about people, fairness and accountability, not only cost.

questions.scenario: Claude keeps writing 800-word answers for Joel at Relecloud when he wants a few sentences. His prompt says, "Don't be too wordy."
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Repeat "don't be wordy" several times in the prompt so that the instruction carries more weight.
options.B: Say concretely what you want: "Answer in three sentences or fewer."
options.C: Ask Claude to explain why its answers are so long, so it becomes aware of the problem and adjusts.
options.D: Switch to the most capable model, which is better at judging the right length for each question.

questions.explanation: Vague or negative instructions leave room for interpretation. Saying what you want, with a concrete measure, is more reliable than saying what to avoid.

why_incorrect.A: Repetition does not define what length is acceptable.
why_incorrect.C: An explanation does not change the next output; a clear instruction does.
why_incorrect.D: Model choice does not fix an unclear length requirement.

questions.scenario: Claude's weekly sales summaries for VanArsdel Foods are inconsistent: sometimes a table, sometimes prose, and regional figures are occasionally missing.
questions.question: Which TWO prompt changes target the root causes?

options.A: List the required regions explicitly and ask Claude to write "no data" when a region is missing from the input.
options.B: Remove the regional breakdown from the input, so Claude has less data to handle and the summary is simpler and more uniform.
options.C: Use a fresh chat each day, so that earlier summaries in the conversation do not influence the structure of the new one.
options.D: Add a line asking Claude to be more consistent this week and to keep the same style as the previous summaries.
options.E: Specify an exact output structure, for example a table with fixed columns and a three-bullet commentary.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent format comes from an unspecified structure; missing items come from unstated completeness requirements. Specify both explicitly, including how to handle gaps.

why_incorrect.B: Removing data makes the summary less complete, not more.
why_incorrect.C: Changing chats does not define format or completeness.
why_incorrect.D: A general request does not define what consistency means.

questions.scenario: A Contoso Health analyst asks Claude in a Project to answer questions from uploaded clinic procedures. Claude sometimes answers from general knowledge instead of the procedures, giving advice that differs from local practice.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Ask questions in shorter sentences.
options.B: Turn on memory so that, over time, Claude learns the clinic's procedures from the questions staff ask.
options.C: In the Project instructions, require answers only from the procedures, with quotes, and a clear note when they do not cover the question.
options.D: Upload general medical reference textbooks as well, so Claude has a fuller picture and relies less on its own general knowledge.

questions.explanation: When answers must reflect specific documents, say so explicitly, require quotes and give Claude permission to say the documents do not cover something. This reduces reliance on general knowledge.

why_incorrect.A: Question length does not determine which source Claude relies on.
why_incorrect.B: Memory does not replace explicit grounding in the approved documents.
why_incorrect.D: More general material increases the chance of answers that differ from local procedures.

questions.scenario: Claude drafts excellent first-round interview summaries for Northwind Lending's HR team, but consistently rates every candidate as a "strong hire", even when the interviewer's notes are negative.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause, and the best fix?

options.A: A faster model would be less generous, because slower models spend more effort finding positives.
options.B: No rating rubric was defined; give criteria with examples per level and ask Claude to cite the notes behind each rating.
options.C: The interview notes are too long, so Claude reads mainly the opening section, which tends to be positive.
options.D: Claude is designed to describe people positively, so it cannot give negative assessments of candidates.

questions.explanation: Ratings drift towards generic positivity when standards are undefined. A rubric with examples for each level, plus evidence for each rating, anchors judgements in the notes. Humans still make the hiring decision.

why_incorrect.A: Speed does not affect leniency; criteria do.
why_incorrect.C: The summaries are otherwise accurate, so the notes are being read.
why_incorrect.D: Claude can give critical assessments when given clear criteria; the gap is the missing rubric.

questions.scenario: A team lead at Alpine Ski House wants a quick checklist for diagnosing a poor Claude response.
questions.question: Which first question is most useful?

options.A: Did my prompt give Claude the context, task, format and constraints it needed?
options.B: Did I phrase the request politely enough for Claude to make its best effort?
options.C: Is the model having a technical problem today, and would trying again later give a better response?
options.D: Was the response long enough to cover the topic in sufficient detail?

questions.explanation: Most underperformance traces back to the prompt or inputs. Checking for missing context, unclear tasks, unspecified formats and unstated constraints resolves the majority of issues.

why_incorrect.B: Politeness is fine but does not supply missing requirements.
why_incorrect.C: Outages are rare; most poor outputs trace to missing context or unclear instructions.
why_incorrect.D: Length is only one aspect and may not be the problem at all.

questions.scenario: Readers of Fabrikam Retail's internal newsletter, drafted with Claude, say the articles are too formal. The editor wants to adjust.
questions.question: What is the best next step?

options.A: Keep the formal style, because it is safer for company-wide communication and readers will adjust to it over time.
options.B: Ask readers to get used to the formal style.
options.C: Update the instructions with the new tone guidance and examples, then check the next issue against reader feedback.
options.D: Stop using Claude for the newsletter, since a tone problem shows it cannot match the company's culture.

questions.explanation: Feedback should change the configuration that produces the output. Updating instructions with examples and checking the effect closes the loop.

why_incorrect.A: The goal is a newsletter people read; feedback indicates a gap.
why_incorrect.B: This places the burden on readers rather than fixing the output.
why_incorrect.D: The tone is adjustable; abandoning the tool is unnecessary.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's tasting-room team has used a Claude-drafted visitor FAQ for a month. Staff note that three questions are often asked but missing, and two answers are often misunderstood.
questions.question: Which TWO adjustments are most appropriate?

options.A: Ask Claude to add 50 more likely questions, so that the FAQ anticipates everything visitors could possibly ask.
options.B: Remove the FAQ and return to relying on staff knowledge, since the gaps show the document cannot keep up with visitors' questions.
options.C: Rewrite the two misunderstood answers with Claude, testing the new wording with a few staff before publishing.
options.D: Keep the misunderstood answers because they are technically accurate.
